toelichting: Eén of twee zinnen per wijnhuis uit de lopende tekst van Decanters jaargangs- en proefverslagen. Een zin over de streek zegt iets over duizend wijnen; een zin over het domein zegt iets over de fles in je hand. Alleen huizen waarvan hetzelfde artikel ook een wijn toont tellen mee: dat sluit toevallige naamgelijkenis uit, want San Polo is in Montalcino ook een gehucht. Elke bloktag in het artikel is een alineagrens, zodat een kop niet aan de zin erna vastplakt; een kop die niets anders is dan een huisnaam geldt als onderwerp voor de alinea die er direct op volgt, want Decanters portretten zetten de naam boven de tekst en herhalen hem er niet in. Weggegooid zijn navigatie- en nieuwsbriefteksten, opsommingen van drie of meer namen, zinnen zonder werkwoord, zinnen die met een verwijswoord of een kleine letter beginnen, en alles met een prijs, een medaille of een puntenscore erin. Van 2556 geoogste zinnen bleven er 1162 over. De proefnotities van Decanter zitten achter hun betaalmuur en hun scores zijn afbeeldingen; hier staat alleen publiek geserveerde lopende tekst, en geen enkel cijfer.

Ceretto.zin: In terms of personal preferences, Ceretto’s Brunate was among my favourites for its sheer, undemanding drinking pleasure.

Sandrone.zin: I was also charmed by Luciano Sandrone’s Le Vigne, the most gorgeously textured and perfumed wine on the table.

E Pira & Figli.zin: ‘I was in full experimental mode,’ recalls E Pira & Figli’s Chiara Boschis of the 1996 vintage.

Albino Rocca.zin: That said, one of my top wines – Albino Rocca’s gorgeous Ronchi – is located on the village’s eastern flank.

Produttori del Barbaresco.zin: Conversely, Produttori del Barbaresco’s bottling was a stunning demonstration.

Giuseppe Cortese.zin: Bruno Giacosa and Ca’ del Baio in the former, and Giuseppe Cortese in the latter are among my top picks.

Paitin.zin: Paitin, Sorì Paitin Vecchie Vigne, Barbaresco Serraboella: Its signature austerity is just sufficiently curbed without sacrificing longevity.

Brezza.zin: As for individual producers, this is not the first time that a wine from Brezza comes out on top in a Decanter panel tasting, and I dare say it won’t be the last either.
Enzo Brezza has transformed this estate, introducing organic methods to realise the full potential of some excellently sited vineyards.
Brezza, Vigna Bricco, Barolo Sarmassa: Mature though not tertiary in nuances while steely tannins have yet to yield.

Massolino.zin: Though Massolino is most famous for his great Vigna Rionda bottling, the Parafada rarely misses a beat, offering a typical Serralunga deep, brooding personality and lots of Nebbiolo purity and perfume.

Cordero di Montezemolo.zin: There are sexier names in Barolo, but Cordero di Montezemolo is one of the most dependable, solid producers in the region.

Paolo Scavino.zin: While some growers, such as Giacomo Fenocchio, Boglietti and Paolo Scavino, made their full range of wines, others had to make some big decisions.

Aldo Conterno.zin: Giacomo Conterno of the Aldo Conterno estate noted: ‘The Nebbiolo was beautifully ripe but one had to avoid excessive ripeness that could give cooked aromas and flavours.
Tasted earlier this year, Aldo Conterno’s Cicala is a wonderfully evocative rendering.

Bartolo Mascarello.zin: A phenomenon more often seen during the height of the summer, Maria-Teresa Mascarello at Bartolo Mascarello, in the Barolo township, recalls that, ‘we harvested in the dust.
Brovia calculates 50% loss of Garblèt Sue’ in the Altenasso MGA, while Bartolo Mascarello reports damage in prime parcels of Cannubi and Rocche dell’Annunziata.
Bartolo Mascarello, Barolo 2016: A co-fermentation of multiple plots, this ageworthy Barolo is a classic in the truest sense.
Of these, Bartolo Mascarello and Giuseppe Rinaldi’s savoury 2022s are worth seeking out.

GB Burlotto.zin: At GB Burlotto in Verduno, the estate’s Barolo Monvigliero spent 33 months ageing in large oak barrels – a sign of the vintage’s quality, according to fifth-generation winemaker Fabio Alessandria.
GB Burlotto’s newest bottling has garnered attention for the MGA, but 2021 offers many convincing efforts including those from Sara Vezza and Fortemasso.

Prunotto.zin: Prunotto’s winemaker Gianluca Torrengo reports that ‘while in Barolo there were 90-100mm of rain, only 40mm fell in Barbaresco’, and furthermore, ‘in an area ranging from Cannubi [Barolo commune] to Fontanafredda [4km to its northeast], there was also hail’.
Prunotto, Vigna Colonnello, Barolo Riserva Bussia: Personality wins over sheer force, but this is not lacking in backbone.

Vietti.zin: Vietti, Barolo: While not actually the least expensive Barolo, what it delivers for the money is exceptional.

Krause has handed the management of Vietti to its former owner Luca Currado to ensure continuity, while Réva and Castello di Perno have turned to Gianluca Colombo, who perfectly represents the link between advancing innovation and tradition.

Castello di Verduno.zin: Castello di Verduno, Barolo: A flagbearer for the village of Verduno; as accessible in price as it is in drinkability.

GD Vajra.zin: GD Vajra, Albe, Barolo: When ‘young vines’ means three decades in the ground… This is much more than just a straightforward ‘entry’ Barolo.

Palladino.zin: Palladino, Barolo Serralunga d’Alba: One of the most consistent village bottlings that is so satisfyingly Serralunga.

Mauro Molino.zin: Mauro Molino, Barolo: Despite a pinch from Monforte, this is so elegantly La Morra-esque.

Giuseppe Rinaldi.zin: Besides top picks such as Aldo Conterno’s Colonnello and Giuseppe Rinaldi’s bottling, the lesser-known Cascina Amalia and Marrone are worth seeking out.
At the Giuseppe Rinaldi estate, ‘we eventually had to replant 70% of our Brunate’, Marta Rinaldi explains, as the vines simply didn’t recover.
Carlotta Rinaldi at Giuseppe Rinaldi acknowledges that they could make a separate Ravera bottling, ‘but we don’t feel it is harmonious on its own,’ she explains.

Domenico Clerico.zin: Prime examples are E Pira & Figli’s’ Mosconi and Domenico Clerico’s Ciabot Mentin Ginestra.

Bruno Giacosa.zin: Bruno Giacosa, Barolo Falletto: Innate refinement is already evident here but delaying gratification will vastly improve enjoyment.
Bruno Giacosa’s red-label wines are among the world’s most collectible.
Ratcheting it up a few notches, Bruno Giacosa and Sandrone’s bottlings from the Valmaggiore cru were two of my top picks of the entire report.
One of the vintage’s greatest wines, Bruno Giacosa’s Rocche del Falletto has consistently offered immense pleasure since age 18.

Azelia.zin: Azelia has just launched a new bottling from Cerretta, both Luigi Einaudi and Scarpa have a Monvigliero on the horizon and Francesco Rinaldi will release a Rocche dell’Annunziata starting with the 2018 vintage.
Azelia’s 2022 is a little bit richer but still in the same vein, and both boast excellent value.

Azelia’s Voghera Riserva (in bond £87.50 Berry Bros & Rudd) and Ceretto’s Cannubi San Lorenzo (in bond £919-£945/magnum Crop & Vine, Ideal Wine Co, VinQuinn) made a strong case for old vines in difficult years.

Oddero.zin: In terms of quantity, a lot of producers are releasing still-older Riserva: Oddero’s Vignarionda 2014, Domenico Clerico’s PerCristina 2011, Parusso’s Oro 2000.
Oddero, Barolo Riserva Vignarionda: Properly austere without being severe, it is a masterful example of vintage and site.

Fontanafredda.zin: Fontanafredda, Barolo Riserva: This classic blend of historic vineyards is settling into its groove.

Mauro Veglio.zin: Mauro Veglio, Barolo Riserva Rocche dell’Annunziata: Barrique ageing has already softened the tannins in this seductively styled Riserva.

Elio Altare.zin: Elio Altare, Vigna Bricco, Barolo Cerretta: The innate balance is already palpable here, promising harmonious ageing.

Travaglini.zin: Travaglini’s Coste della Sesia is a beautiful snapshot of the fine-boned, fragrant expression of Nebbiolo found in north Piedmont’s cool, sub-alpine reaches.

La Gironda.zin: La Gironda, Oddero and Olim Bauda are names to look for here.

Stefano Occhetti.zin: Stefano Occhetti is an excellent example of this new generation.

Monte Maletto.zin: A new generation is braving the elements, too, with boutique projects – one, Monte Maletto, captures the alpine character and delicacy of Carema.

Antoniolo.zin: Antoniolo has also been making consistently solid wines in recent decades, and the family’s Osso San Grato site stands alongside the greatest crus of the Langhe.

Gian Luca Colombo.zin: Gian Luca Colombo’s Meretto is another must-try if you can find it.

Elvio Cogno.zin: As Valter Fissore at Elvio Cogno states: ‘It is supposed to be a friendly wine for drinking chilled in the summer.’

Giacomo Conterno.zin: However, despite coming from the mediocre 1987 vintage, Giacomo Conterno’s Monfortino Barolo Riserva made a lasting impression.

And, as prices were already soaring for the three ‘big Gs’ – Giacomo Conterno, Bruno Giacosa and Gaja – aficionados started seeking out treasures among (then) lesser-known estates such as Cavallotto, GD Vajra and GB Burlotto: all highly regarded today.

Muraje.zin: Deborah and Federico Santini of Muraje are emblematic of the fresh young faces that are reversing years of viticultural abandonment.
Despite its diminutive size, Muraje is vital to the preservation of this unique corner of Piedmont.

Fletcher.zin: While the latter is clearly Fletcher’s calling card, he also succeeds with a characterful Arneis, Pinot-esque Langhe Nebbiolo, and a partial whole-cluster Barbera.
Fletcher resigned from Ceretto earlier this year but is extremely deferential.

Margherita Otto.zin: This is the model he emulates for his own Barolo Margherita Otto, which he started making commercially in 2015.

Tenuta Santa Caterina.zin: He purchased the derelict Tenuta Santa Caterina and has restored it to its former glory.

La Raia.zin: When the Rossi Cairo family purchased La Raia in late 2002, the centuries-old aristocratic estate was selling bulk wine.

La Barbatella.zin: Produced since 1983, La Barbatella is a benchmark for unoaked Barbera d’Asti.

Francesco Iandolo.zin: Francesco Iandolo makes just two wines – a Nizza and a Timorasso.

Borgogno.zin: Earlier this year, Borgogno’s Riserva was the highlight at a 10-year release retrospective.

Fratelli Alessandria.zin: Others, such as Fratelli Alessandria’s Monvigliero were evolving more harmoniously.

Tibaldi.zin: Daniela Tibaldi is one of a number of producers, however, who believes that 2016 will be even better.

Il Poggione.zin: For Il Poggione, the Bindocci family was convinced by the balance of structure and elegance that their old-vine Riserva cru Vigna Paganelli demonstrated.
‘You had to pick around the rains,’ recalls Francesca Bindocci at Il Poggione, adding that it’s a vintage which shows who worked well in the vineyard throughout the year.
Il Poggione (95): With a production of 200,000 bottles, this is an excellent ambassador for the region and vintage.

Biondi-Santi.zin: Most of the 2020 Riserva are overshadowed by Le Chiuse and Biondi-Santi’s stellar late-release Riservas – 2016 and 2019 respectively – but my top two picks come from the 2020 vintage, from opposite sides of the region characterised by very different terroirs.

Querciabella.zin: While the dry, hot 2017 vintage was a challenge, Querciabella managed to find balance and was unanimously noted as having the stuffing and framework to make it cellarworthy.
Along with Istine’s inaugual Elle bottling is Fontodi’s newest offering, Pastrolo, and Querciabella’s Gran Selezione now includes fruit from recently acquired holdings there.

Il Molino di Grace.zin: Bibbiano’s Vigna del Capannino allows a sense of place to shine through, and in Il Molino di Grace’s predominantly new barrique-aged Il Margone, the wood is well-integrated.
From Panzano, where Pietraforte (a hard, calcareous sandstone) abounds, Il Molino di Grace and Fontodi’s 2021s are deeply coloured, darkly fruited and amply structured.

Le Cinciole.zin: Nevertheless, it has encouraged Orsini to upgrade Le Cinciole’s Aluigi bottling from Riserva to Gran Selezione with the just released, excellent 2016.

Completing my selection of 90 annata recommendations are half a dozen new releases from 2021, with Le Cinciole and I Fabbri’s Terra di Lamole particularly of note, as well as the excellent 2020 Castell’in Villa.
In the cooler, eastern exposed pocket of the UGA, Le Cinciole’s more chiselled 2019 A Luigi is also worth seeking out.
Le Cinciole, Chianti Classico 2019 Far from an ‘entry-level’ wine, Le Cinciole’s annata is a gorgeous, detailed expression of Panzano.

Poggerino.zin: In Radda, Poggerino’s Piero Lanza had to bring in fruit from more humid plots early – in mid-September – due to the threat of botrytis and acid rot.
Poggerino opted to forgo a Riserva selection this year, to the benefit of the estate’s annata, which is among my top value picks.

Argiano.zin: While prices may have gone up in recent years, the notable increase in quality justifies this – and the estate bottling is still relatively affordable.
In an effort to curb over-concentration Argiano, along with other estates, are also replanting at lower densities.
Argiano (93): 2016 is the best estate bottling of Brunello from Argiano in recent memory.
At Argiano, CEO and winemaker, Bernardino Sani noted the long ripening period between veraison and maturation, describing the resulting grapes as ‘rich in concentration, fruit and colour’.
At Argiano, Bernardino Sani’s greatest concern was ensuring the wine didn’t tire during the long maturation in wood.

Fattoi.zin: A perennial pick, Fattoi is among my favourite wines of the vintage not just for the exceptional value it represents, but also for its palpable sense of place.
Giodo is one of my top picks for the second year in a row and Fattoi joins the ranks, not just for the sheer value it represents but for its palpable sense of place.

Michele Satta.zin: ‘Two weeks of Tramontana wind,’ commented Michele Satta, ‘was most likely the main factor for the quality of the 2016 vintage in Bolgheri.’

Masseto.zin: Masseto is a rare example of a single-vineyard, single-varietal wine, made from 100% Merlot.

Today, carved into the ancient blue clay that makes up the vineyard, the Masseto winery is a physical and symbolic tribute to the estate’s history and rapid evolution, from a humble intuition about the hidden potential of a vineyard site to an internationally acclaimed wine.
Masseto has received international acclaim since its birth in 1986.
Tasting Masseto 2019, the broad shoulders of the wine were immediately clear, with outstanding grapey tannins enriched by fine-tuned oak.

We worked with extraction to manage the concentration,’ says Gaia Cinnirella, Masseto’s winemaker, explaining that during the 2023 harvest period, they tasted the grapes in the vineyards every day, and picked plot by plot.

Le Crocine.zin: In 2016, Marzichi Lenzi released his first Bolgheri Superiore, Le Crocine’s 57022, which is one of the top wines in its lower price range given his almost exclusively local reputation.

Mulini di Segalari.zin: Ai Confini del Bosco, from the Mulini di Segalari estate, is possibly the least costly wine in Bolgheri (€16-18 RRP).

Tenuta San Guido.zin: The 2018 Sassicaia is the 50th edition officially produced by Tenuta San Guido (although the marquise has bottled it since 1948).

Carlo Paoli, general manager and production manager at Tenuta San Guido recounts how they had to make a big selection at harvest time and, unusually, ‘we brought in the grapes in the morning and worked in the cellar with the air-con.’

Caccia al Piano.zin: I Greppi is worthy of attention due to improved vineyard management, while Caccia al Piano is now bottling their Bolgheri Superiore exclusively from the outstanding vineyard of San Biagio, close to the historical vineyard of Sassicaia.

Ornellaia.zin: Lamberto Frescobaldi (president of Frescobaldi Wines, which owns both Ornellaia and Masseto) told me earlier this year: ‘People are focusing on the variety [Cabernet Franc]; you have to focus on the site.’
Marco Balsimelli, Ornellaia and Masseto’s new production director, agrees: ‘The 2022 character is more concentrated than the 2021.’
This was followed by the announcement in September that Ornellaia’s CEO, Giovanni Geddes da Filicaja, would be retiring imminently.

Ornellaia’s winemaker, Olga Fusari has been replaced by Denise Cosentino, a Calabrian who has spent the past seven years working for Domaines Barons de Rothschild in China, most recently at Domaine de Long Dai.
Pruning at Ornellaia, meanwhile, was only completed two weeks ago.

Ornellaia was one of the first Italian wineries to employ Simonit & Sirch, who pioneered a way of pruning that has since caught on among some of the most revered estates in the world – as well as ambitious smaller estates.
The 11ha of vines at Masseto are much more manageable than Ornellaia’s 134ha, and so the former is managed with a completely organic programme, although it’s not certified.

The older vintages Marco chooses to open at both Ornellaia and Masseto are years with similar conditions to 2021 and – in the case of Ornellaia – similar blends, yet the refinement of the winemaking process from then to now is striking.

Donne Fittipaldi.zin: Donne Fittipaldi’s ‘Magnetic’ Bolgheri Rosso (Cabernet Franc aged in amphorae and cocciopesto) is a benchmark in this regard.

Grattamacco.zin: Marrone notes that ‘the pH [of Grattamacco 2021] is very low – 3.56’, while Gaja’s Ca’Marcanda estate recorded ‘an average pH of 3.3 and acidity levels of 7g/l.’

Guado al Tasso.zin: At Guado al Tasso, new plantings are trained higher off the ground to allow more air to circulate and prevent diseases such as peronospera.
Guado al Tasso takes this to the next level by using Vermentino clones from Corsica, which I’m told have more aromatic potential than the traditional Tuscan Vermentino.

Val di Suga.zin: Val di Suga, a single site specialist, produced a beautifully fresh Brunello from its Spuntali vineyard.

Castello Banfi.zin: Meanwhile, Castello Banfi’s 2004 is the best Brunello I’ve tried from the Mariani family for its punch, typicity, accessibility and staying power.

Col di Lamo.zin: Other smaller, and essentially brand new, estates such as Gianna Neri’s Col di Lamo and the Terzuoli family’s SassodiSole in Montalcino’s still very unfashionable Torrenieri showed no newcomers’ nerves.

San Polino.zin: Further south, the Loacker family’s Corte Pavone and San Polino were especially notable for being among the very few certified organic or biodynamic estates in Montalcino in 2004.
San Polino’s conscientious vineyard practises surpass organic and biodynamic protocols, and the wines are expressively pure Sangiovese.

Fattoria dei Barbi.zin: Historic estates in the warmer south like Fattoria dei Barbi and Ciacci Piccolomini showed the value of old school winemaking practises, guiding rather than dictating ferments, leading to open-knit Brunellos whose soft autumnal flavours flow.

Le Potazzine.zin: In a not dissimilar stylistic vein was Tenuta Le Potazzine, made by duo Gigliola Giannetti and Giuseppe Gorelli, the latter a Montalcino-based winemaking consultant.

Casanova di Neri.zin: ‘You really felt this in the north,’ says Gianlorenzo Neri at Casanova di Neri, where he cites temperatures of 29°C in the day versus 14 to 15°C at night.

Fuligni.zin: Fuligni produced the top wine for me in 2016 – elegant in its power with great complexity and the vintage’s radiant acidity.

Canalicchio di Sopra.zin: Both Padelletti and Canalicchio di Sopra were among those who harvested mid- to late-September – essentially the same timing as in other recent vintages.
Despite a striking new bottling from Montosoli, it was the estate’s classic Brunello that I was particularly taken with.

San Polo.zin: At San Polo, the winery’s two single vineyards are side by side.

Marilisa Allegrini’s Montalcino property has gone from strength to strength since the arrival of winemaker Riccardo Fratton in 2015, with the introduction of two single-vineyard bottlings the same year and organic certification as of 2017.

Gianni Brunelli.zin: Pretty fragrances, freshness and deftly managed tannins are among the highlights of this estate’s 2017.

Il Marroneto.zin: Alessandro Mori’s Madonna delle Grazie is one of the top wines of the vintage and his estate bottling isn’t far behind.
Both are a tribute to tireless work in the vineyard and faithfulness to his naturalista philosophy.

Le Ragnaie.zin: Riccardo Campinoti’s Casanovina Montosoli is the finest of his solid 2017 lineup.
Of note too, is the first Brunello release from his Passo del Lume Spento vineyard, which sits at over 600 metres.
Riccardo Campinoti (Le Ragnaie), however, recalls that ‘there weren’t big problems’.

Poggio di Sotto.zin: The 2017 annata still captures Poggio di Sotto’s style and the 2016 Riserva is worthy of its category.
Podere Le Ripi, Poggio Antico and Poggio di Sotto are among these examples.

San Filippo.zin: San Filippo, La Lucère One of my top wines of the vintage, La Lucère has reached an extraordinary level of elegance without sacrificing substance and structure for ageing.

Valdicava.zin: For Vincenzo Abbruzzese at Valdicava, who calls 2019 ‘a fairy-tale vintage with an American ending,’ the only challenge was sacrificing 2018.

Le Chiuse.zin: ‘It was hard to make bad Brunello in 2019,’ Le Chiuse’s Lorenzo Magnelli declared – and yet, some did.

Baricci.zin: Then there is Baricci’s Nello, which seems wholly laden with fruit until a complex structure matrix takes hold.

Capanna.zin: Capanna and Padelletti are more elegantly sculpted yet still decidedly firm.

Talenti.zin: According to Riccardo Talenti (Talenti), whose vineyards are in the south, deciding when to pick was the most challenging aspect of the year.

Padelletti.zin: Le Chiuse and Padelletti are more finely framed but not lacking depth.

Altesino.zin: Upfront in its attractions and should be enjoyed when all of these are in their exuberant prime.

Lisini.zin: In the case of Lisini’s promising new wine, Poggio Severo is a direct response to the changing climate.

Castello Romitorio.zin: Other wines built along graceful lines are Castello Romitorio, Tassi’s Giuseppe Tassi, Talenti and Val di Suga.

Capezzana.zin: To celebrate the 40th anniversary of Trefiano – Tenuta di Capezzana ’s stunning take on Carmignano Riserva – a vertical tasting of a handful of vintages ranging from 1988 to 2019 (the current release) was held in Florence this February.
Of the 20 or so producers in this small, 116-hectare DOCG, Tenuta di Capezzana – owned by the Contini Bonacossi family – is at the top of the heap.
Since 2008, Trefiano has been farmed organically, and the entire Capezzana estate received organic certification in 2015.

Rocca di Montegrossi.zin: According to Marco Ricasoli-Firidolfi at Rocca di Montegrossi in Gaiole, ‘from Christmas of 2019 until the end of May, precipitation was a rare occurrence.’

Castagnoli.zin: Tim Schefenacker at Castagnoli added that there were five days in July that reached 43°C.
In the UGA of Castellina, Castagnoli has finally brought its top bottling into the Chianti Classico fold.

Podere Poggio Scalette.zin: Exemplifying this are wines like Bibbiano, Podere Poggio Scalette and Montesecondo.

Isole e Olena.zin: Isole e Olena’s excellent 2021 is all this – with extra tautness.

Monte Bernardi.zin: Monte Bernardi was down a whopping 80%, whereas Le Cinciole estimates a more modest shortfall of 10-15%, for example.

Istine.zin: Vigna Istine and Vigna Cavarchione (respectively from Radda and Gaiole) are among my top wines of the vintage and clearly belong at the apex of Chianti Classico’s pyramid.
I was also privy to a stunning sneak peek of Istine’s collection, which includes two new Gran Selezione – one from Lamole and the other from Vagliagli.
In the upper echelon, Istine’s 2021 Riserva is equal in quality to the estate’s trio of Gran Selezione – just different in concept.
Istine: Angela Fronti’s annata is one of Chianti Classico’s best value wines, and her vineyard selections are among the region’s top examples.
Istine, Chianti Classico 2018: Mostly Radda fruit with a little bit from Gaiole, this is one of the region’s best-value Chianti Classicos.

Terreno.zin: On Macigno (non-calcareous sandstone) soil conversely, Terreno’s 2020 Asofia caresses with softer, finer tannins, though is not lacking in a plush core.
Terreno, Sillano, Chianti Classico Gran Selezione 2019: The first ever vintage of this single-vineyard selection from up-and-comer, Sofia Ruhne is a stunner.

Fontodi.zin: Fontodi’s Vigna del Sorbo is particularly emblematic but executes this with unbelievable refinement.

Castello di Ama.zin: Notable exceptions include Castello di Ama’s 2020 single-vineyard La Casuccia and Bellavista bottlings – the latter is one of two wines which received my highest score of the entire Chianti Classico report this year.

Monteraponi.zin: Particularly impressive was Monteraponi’s first ever Gran Selezione – ‘ Il Bragantino’ – which sits alongside Bellavista at the top of my rankings.

Antinori.zin: ‘These won’t change the balance sheet at Antinori,’ notes technical director Dora Pacciani.
Antinori’s new bottlings are truly exciting – I was particularly impressed with the San Sano from Gaiole.
One of the first was Antinori, whose 1971 Tignanello was a Sangiovese and Cabernet Sauvignon blend from the Chianti Classico subzone, but declassified to Vino da Tavola.

Isola delle Falcole.zin: Equally notable is Isola delle Falcole’s fifth-ever vintage from a vineyard in the wilds of Panzano.

La Montanina.zin: Top achievers, such as Poggerino, Monteraponi’s Il Campitello and La Montanina have the potential for 15 years in the cellar.

Tregole.zin: At Tregole, both the Riserva and the Gran Selezione are crafted from single vineyards.

Tenuta di Arceno.zin: Further north in the district, Tenuta di Arceno is gentler in expression owing in part to vineyards on non-calcareous sandstone soil known as ‘ macigno ‘.

La Vigna di San Martino ad Argiano.zin: Furthermore, boutique producer, Maurizio Alongi and promising newcomer, La Vigna di San Martino ad Argiano have selected the Riserva category for the sole Chianti Classico each produces.

Castello di Monsanto.zin: Laura Bianchi at Castello di Monsanto, confirms that they have not experienced a decreased demand for Riserva since the Gran Selezione category was introduced.
Castello di Monsanto: This renowned estate shows a steady progression across Chianti Classico’s three categories in the 2016, 2017 and 2018 vintages.

San Giusto a Rentennano.zin: Finally, from one of the region’s warmer pockets, San Giusto a Rentennano’s 2022 Le Baròncole is impressive.

San Felice.zin: A stalwart for value, and readily available, San Felice’s annata is the quintessential well priced, mid-week Chianti Classico.

Tua Rita.zin: ‘It shines for its versatility,’ notes D’Attoma, who worked with prominent Suvereto estate Tua Rita to craft Keir, the most groundbreaking among at least a dozen new-wave Syrahs fermenting in Tuscan terracotta amphorae.

Caiarossa.zin: Syrah and Cabernet Franc are the key varieties of Caiarossa, a trailblazing wine that embodies the prevailing urge to pursue distinctiveness even when bringing together different grapes in blends.

Bertinga.zin: Bertinga’s Volta di Bertinga and La Massa’s Asiram – both made under the supervision of legendary Bordeaux winemaker Stéphane Derenoncourt – show a UGA-like connection to the sub-zone of origin.

Le Mortelle.zin: This year celebrating the 50th anniversary of the launch of Tignanello, Antinori has conducted thorough experiments at Le Mortelle in coastal Maremma, where the pivot is Cabernet Franc for Poggio alle Nane and Carmenère for Ampio.

Petrolo.zin: Monteraponi’s Trebbiano, first bottled in 2012 from vines in Radda in Chianti, and Petrolo’s Bòggina B, first produced in 2014 from clones of 1970s plantings in Valdarno di Sopra, are both fundamental to Trebbiano Toscano’s comeback.

Fattoria Le Pupille.zin: One wine which defies the perception of Tuscany as lacking in fine white wines is Fattoria Le Pupille’s Piemme, a thrilling Petit Manseng from the 1ha Pian di Fiora vineyard on the coastal hills of Tuscany’s Maremma.

Belguardo.zin: President of the Maremma Toscana consorzio Francesco Mazzei is spearheading the Superiore initiative with his family’s Belguardo estate, releasing V 2021 (formerly ‘Codice V’) as one of the first wines to be labelled Vermentino Superiore.

Tenuta di Ghizzano.zin: Ginevra Venerosi Pesciolini of Tenuta di Ghizzano, in the Maremma, is also doing exciting things with Vermentino, although in this case she labels it as Costa Toscana.

Tenuta Gracciano della Seta.zin: After tasting the wines blind, my top 2015s were Metinella, Tenuta Gracciano della Seta, Avignonesi and Poliziano’s Asinone.

Salcheto.zin: Though not dissatisfied with the vintage, Michele Manelli at Salcheto admits to being a bit squeezed, saying that the vines never completely caught up after the cooler temperatures early in the summer.

Il Molinaccio.zin: Marco Malavasi at Il Molinaccio concurs, asserting that ‘2018 was a good year but not good enough to produce a Riserva.’
Il Molinaccio, La Spinosa, Vino Nobile di Montepulciano 2019: From a cool pocket of Montepulciano, this is textured, crunchy and pure with huge drinkability.

Boscarelli.zin: Nevertheless, there were some pleasant surprises, and both Boscarelli and Dei even managed to capture Sangiovese’s beautiful aromatic intricacies.
First to 2019, which Luca De Ferrari at Boscarelli describes as a balanced year.
Boscarelli, Vino Nobile di Montepulciano 2019: Fleshy, chewy, racy and nuanced – simply one of the best straight up Vino Nobiles I have tasted.
Despite losing some production to late-season hail, Boscarelli was a standout yet again this year.
‘It was an abnormal frost,’ states Boscarelli’s Luca De Ferrari, explaining that it also hit vineyards at higher elevations.

Tenuta Trerose.zin: Boscarelli has coaxed out admirable elegance, and Tenuta Trerose charms with its succulence.

Pol Roger.zin: ‘Pol Roger became one of the big three Champagne brands in London during the 1870s,’ explains James Simpson MW of Pol Roger UK.
‘Whether he had money or not, Churchill continued buying Pol Roger throughout his life,’ he adds, hinting that Churchill may have consumed – or at least ordered – as many as 42,000 bottles.

Charles Heidsieck.zin: This was one of the rare vintages of the revived Charles Heidsieck Champagne Charlie cuvée, which I was lucky enough to taste when I visited Charles Heidsieck.

Aurélien Suenen.zin: Aurélien Suenen is pouring vins clairs, the still base wines from the 2023 harvest that have yet to become sparkling Champagne.

Pierre Péters.zin: Pierre Péters’ Les Chétillons Grand Cru 2009 was cream of the crop.

Laurent-Perrier.zin: Laurent-Perrier’s Alexandra rosé is the perfect example of this; an icon of its style.

Château Ste Roseline.zin: Château Ste Roseline is as much visited for its 12th century abbey, the mummified remains of Ste Roseline and its contemporary art collection as for its wine.

Château Galoupet.zin: The few exceptions among the cru classé estates are Clos Cibonne, Château Galoupet, and the top wines of Château St-Martin and Château St-Maur.
Château Galoupet is a Provence cru classé estate on the southern slopes of the Massif des Maures, overlooking the Mediterranean and the island of Porquerolles.

In April 2022, Galoupet launched its first two new rosés: Château Galoupet cru classé rosé and a second wine, Nomade (made from estate grapes in 2021, but to be made in future years with grapes from partner growers who follow regenerative viticulture).
After trialling different rosé blends, the 2021 Château Galoupet cru classé is primarily Grenache.
The Château Galoupet cru classé rosé comes in a 70% recycled glass bottle, which has a feuille morte colour.

Domaine Maubernard.zin: Though the one 2016 wine (Domaine Maubernard) did have the biggest tannic structure of all, reflecting the traditional vision of Bandol reds as being ageworthy, most of the reds were showing much greater youthful accessibility than Bandols of decades past.

Château Canadel.zin: Others, namely Château Canadel and Peyraud’s Domaine Tempier, have a more traditional, intense tannic structure.

Domaine de la Font des Pères.zin: Most producers use large old foudres, but a few are using new oak such as Château Vannières and Domaine de la Font des Pères whose wines have a modern, almost New World appeal, while the presence of Cinsault in a blend adds vivacity.

Château de Pibarnon.zin: Château de Pibarnon’s Nuances and Bégude’s l’Irreductible are both almost entirely Mourvèdre.

L’Irreductble is a serious, unoaked, dark pink-red, while Eric de St Victor of Château de Pibarnon, recognising that Mourvèdre rosé takes time to open up, ages his Nuances in stoneware which gives tension and purity, before releasing the wine with a year’s age.

Domaine Tempier.zin: It certainly seems criminal to shout about drinking Domaine Tempier’s rosé as soon as it is launched when it ages so splendidly.

Domaine Marie Berenice.zin: Damian Roux of Domaine Marie Berenice has observed that there is a growing interest in white wine, but is faced with a logistics dilemma: if the trend changes again, he will be left with too much white and there is only so much the rosés can absorb in the blend.

Château Sainte Marguerite.zin: Château Sainte Marguerite’s total production is split between 70% rosé, 15% white and 15% red, but Olivier commented that now, with greater distribution, they ‘will obviously further increase the share of rosé that corresponds to global demand’.
Giron added that the range of Château Sainte Marguerite wines will evolve, rather than grow in total volume, and over the next two years there will be a complete redesign of the range.

Domaines Ott.zin: One of the best-known producers in Provence, Domaines Ott remains modest; its quality is high but there is little of the marketing razzmatazz of other high-profile estates.

Château Vignelaure.zin: Eloi Dürrbach, who made the wine at Château Vignelaure and then set up his own estate, Domaine de Trévallon, continued to make an equal blend of Cabernet and Syrah under the IGP Bouches-du-Rhône.

Château Bellini.zin: He is currently restructuring and re-planting his new estate, Château Bellini, formerly Domaine de Fontlade, outside of Brignoles, and he even introduced his friend George Clooney to a neighbouring estate.
During a visit in 2021, Château Bellini was a busy building site.

A great lover of art and opera, Bove renamed this domaine Château Bellini, after the opera composer Vincenzo Bellini and the Venetian painter Giovanni Bellini (he had already named his dog Bellini, too).

Henschke.zin: Stephen and Prue Henschke, fifth-generation producers of some of South Australia ’s most iconic wines, are only too familiar with the annual roll of the dice.

Cirillo.zin: The world’s oldest-producing Grenache vines are on Marco Cirillo’s Nuriootpa vineyard in the Barossa, planted in 1848.

Yalumba.zin: As a consequence, Yalumba presents an expansive range, highlighting differences between ancient vines (bush vines planted in 1889), to those planted in the late 1940s and late ‘80s, as well as ‘newer’ plantings from 35 years old.
Yalumba winery was established in 1849 by Samuel Smith, whose success as a gold prospector bolstered his fledgling Barossa Valley property.
One eye is focused respectfully on Yalumba’s history, while the other focuses on the future of a medium-sized wine company with ambitions to have its best wines regarded more seriously.
As Australia’s oldest family-owned winery, Yalumba is acutely aware of its place on the world stage.

It also established a vine nursery to propagate less-familiar grape varieties – most notably Viognier, which Yalumba has championed since 1980 – and superior clones to improve underperforming vineyards.

It was Yalumba that helped draft a charter to accurately classify different ages of ‘old’ vines into four definite categories – Old (+35 years), Survivors (+70 years), Centenarians (+100 years) and Ancestors (+125 years).
In the Yalumba playbook, such attention to detail makes a significant difference.

Yalumba has also maintained an extraordinary cellar at its Angaston winery and headquarters – to examine the quality of the company’s own wines as they age, and to store great wines of the world as benchmarks for the education of its winemakers.
Central to this vast wine vault is the Yalumba Museum Collection, which is being issued on 17 May as a milestone anniversary celebration.

Both Robert and leading wine critic Andrew Caillard were particularly pleased with the 1974 Yalumba FDR 1A Claret: a model for Yalumba’s extensive history of Cabernet Sauvignon -driven blends with Shiraz.

Bekkers.zin: McLaren Vale viticulturist Toby Bekkers and his winemaker wife Emmanuelle have made Grenache a key feature of their Bekkers wine brand.

Aphelion.zin: The constant in Aphelion’s portfolio is Confluence, which shows off Grenache’s rich savoury mid palate.

Twelftree.zin: Michael Twelftree is another Grenache vineyard hunter who knows elite fruit is difficult to find.

Seppeltsfield.zin: This gesture marked the launch of the magnificent Seppeltsfield bluestone cellar in 1878, a sturdy three-level monument designed and built in 1866 by Benno’s father, Joseph Seppelt, who had brought the family from Silesia in 1849 and established the vineyards in 1851.

They form the backbone of Seppeltsfield fortified wine production, along with old Shiraz and Mourvèdre vines, although precise percentages of each variety in Para tawny was not recorded until the 1980s.
The creation of Seppeltsfield Para in 1878 is also tied to the historical foundation of Australian wine, which thrived on the success of fortified wine production from the colony’s earliest years.
Seppeltsfield Para was produced as a statement of the family’s success, a gesture continued on an annual basis through successive winemakers – and eventually different owners.
Three Seppeltsfield winemakers were present at the tasting – including original family descendent Charlie Seppelt – yet modestly play down their role.
‘These are not my wines,’ says James Godfrey, who joined Seppeltsfield in 1978 and became chief fortified winemaker until Foster’s Group sold Seppeltsfield in 2007.

Eden Hall.zin: But he also makes Riesling for Eden Hall Wines, remaining true to the Vickery winemaking gospel, with all wines stellar examples of poise and purity.

Rieslingfreak.zin: The most enthusiastic purveyors of multiple Riesling expressions are John and Belinda Hughes, whose Rieslingfreak label produces a dozen different styles each vintage, sourced from two regions.

Elderton.zin: With his brother Allister Ashmead, he is co-managing director of Elderton, the Barossa brand founded by their parents in 1982.
Elderton still makes an Estate Cabernet today, but the collector’s favourite is the premium Ashmead Cabernet Sauvignon.
It’s made, in minute quantities, by Elderton’s head of viticulture and winemaking Julie Ashmead (Cameron’s wife) and winemaker Brock Harrison.
Elderton is a true family-run business, with Allister’s wife Rebecca the winery’s export manager who also looks after bottlings.
The premium counterpart to Elderton’s Ashmead Cabernet is the Command Shiraz.
Elderton introduced French oak alongside the American in 1996, reduced fermentation temperatures in 2010 and, since 2013, Command has spent its final year in seasoned (as opposed to new) oak barrels.

Torbreck.zin: Today Hongell is chief winemaker and general manager at Torbreck, a winery that shot to fame in the 1990s by cherry-picking the best of that ‘paddock’.
Hongell admits that, prior to joining Torbreck, he’d not fully appreciated the pedigree of this 85 hectare estate and its 200ha of contract fruit sources.
Hongell joined Torbreck in 2017, by which time the company had changed hands twice.
Speculation was rife that Torbreck would falter without its charismatic founder, but the wines continue to sell out.
Winemaker Scott McDonald – a veteran of 16 Torbreck vintages – is well-versed in the signature grape handling and maturation regime.
Torbreck’s ‘go hard or go home’ methods of late picking and dry farming in a region that sometimes goes without rain for 300 days in a year has given Hongell sleepless nights.
Even at 15 to 15.5% alcohol, Torbreck’s seductively perfumed reds have striking balance, detail and precision.
There are no plans to expand production, although in 2019 Torbreck acquired Escarpment Winery in Martinborough, New Zealand from Larry McKenna, who continues to make its acclaimed Pinot Noir ).
‘Torbreck stands for the preservation of history and sites so we are paying it forward.’

Adelaida.zin: Home of top-quality Paso wine, Adelaida is the westernmost of the sub-districts and closest to the Pacific Ocean.
At its closest point, Adelaida lies just less than 10km from the coast, with the Santa Lucia Range mountains in between the two.
The average rainfall in Adelaida is generally the highest in the Paso region, at 635mm per year, and in 2021 the bulk of the rain came from one late-winter storm.

And as it happens, California’s oldest Pinot Noir plantings south of Sonoma County are in what is now the Adelaida District, in the hills on Paso’s west side: the 59-year-old HMR Vineyard, owned by the Van Steenwyk family’s Adelaida Vineyards & Winery.
Adelaida’s ranch manager emeritus and resident historian Mike Whitener was 13 when the Hoffmans hired his father John, a prominent local farmer, to plant the first vines and manage the ranch.
Under Adelaida Vineyards & Winery, HMR became part of a growing estate vineyard portfolio which the Van Steenwyks had already begun assembling over a massive patchwork of 728ha.
The Adelaida team are the third guardians of HMR now, but its Pinot Noir and Chardonnay are part of California’s vinous heritage still flying under the radar.
One exception to this was Alta Colina in the Adelaida District AVA (American Viticultural Area), which achieved average to slightly above-average yields in 2021.
Home of top-quality Paso wine, Adelaida is the westernmost of the sub-districts and closest to the Pacific ocean.
Just south of Adelaida lies Willow Creek, a high rainfall, high elevation sub-district with similar properties.
Lying closest to the Pacific Ocean, Adelaida District is situated less than 10km from the coast, just over the Santa Lucia Range.
Maha Estate has vineyards positioned right on the border between the Adelaida and Willow Creek sub-districts – the two top-performing zones in 2022 (see ‘sweet spot’ box above).
Adelaida’s HMR vineyard, planted in the 1970s, is the oldest Pinot Noir -producing vineyard on the Central Coast, cited by André Tchelistcheff as ‘a jewel of ecological elements’.

Alta Colina.zin: Molly Lonborg at Alta Colina said: ‘Because of our high elevation, we have a lot of high-intensity fruit, a lot of colour and a lot of tannin.’

Tatomer.zin: Graham Tatomer of Tatomer Wines in Santa Maria, California believes the window of opportunity is largest with Riesling.

McPrice Myers.zin: Aron Nevarez, vineyard manager and head viticulturist for prized brands such as Denner and McPrice Myers, is similarly enthusiastic about the vintage’s potential: ‘Out of the past seven vintages, 2021 is one of my favourite years.’

Epoch Estate.zin: Jordan Fiorentini of Epoch Estate calls 2021 ‘a winemaker’s vintage where we could wait to pick the fruit until we felt it was time, without too many climatic factors getting in the way’.

Tablas Creek.zin: At Tablas Creek’s Adelaida estate vineyard, December was the wettest month on record, receiving 350mm of rain out of the annual total of 500mm.
Tablas Creek had the advantage of being insulated from these issues because it has a year-round crew.
The Haas and Perrin family partnership of Tablas Creek is a good example of personal and practical ambition.

Booker.zin: Similarly, back at Booker, Graves says: ‘The more we have focused on soil health, the more resilient our vines have become.’
Booker’s 35ha Willow Creek District estate vineyard is certified organic and Regenerative Organic Certified (ROC).

Thacher.zin: The choice of rootstocks or own-rooted as per Thacher’s Shell Creek Vineyard Chenin Blanc, row spacing, clonal selection, irrigation techniques and the ability to dry-farm, are just a few of the ongoing areas of research and trial.

Giornata.zin: Thacher, Giornata and Torrin are all husband-and-wife teams bringing up the next generation of Paso people and making wines that speak to both their origin and their audience.

Martín Códax.zin: Katia Alvarez, winemaker at Martín Códax, began producing a lees-aged Albariño – Martín Códax Lías – in 2005.
She explains that for her the Martín Códax Lías 2018 typifies Rías Baixas.

Adegas Galegas.zin: His Adegas Galegas Veigadares 2017 has a backbone of Albariño – sourced from three separate plots in the sub-regions of Salnes Valley, Condado do Tea and O Rosal.

Pazo de Señoráns.zin: However it was the final wine of the tasting, a library vintage of Pazo de Señoráns Selección de Añada 2010, that really stood out in terms of complexity.

Raúl Pérez.zin: With family roots firmly in Spain’s remote northwestern Bierzo region, Raúl Pérez’s minimal-intervention methods and their extraordinary results have rapidly propelled him to the status of global champion.
Raúl Pérez is the archetype of the intuitive winemaking genius.

Albamar.zin: Apart from Señorío de Rubios, other red producers to look out for are Albamar, Attis, Zárate and especially Forjas del Salnés, where Rodri Méndez works with Bierzo superstar Raúl Pérez.

Forjas del Salnes.zin: If anyone qualifies as a cult winemaker in Rías Baixas, then it’s arguably self-effacing Rodri Méndez, who has benefited from the advice of Bierzo’s superstar producer, Raúl Pérez, when it comes to his reds (Goliardo is a total bargain).

Santiago Roma.zin: Everything he makes is delicious, from his Colleita to his estate Albariño to his Selección.

Susana Esteban.zin: Leading winemaker and consultant, Susana Esteban, explains: ‘Portalegre [also a DOC] is completely different from the rest of Alentejo, and Estremoz [in Borba DOC] has nothing to do with Beja [the region’s southern boundary].’

João Portugal Ramos.zin: ‘Private winemakers and wine-growers brought quality and innovation to the region,’ explains João Portugal Ramos, then one of a cohort of highly sought-after young Portuguese consultant winemakers, whose number included Paulo Laureano, Rui Reguinga and Luis Duarte.

Herdade do Rocim.zin: Leading talha exponent Pedro Ribeiro (Herdade do Rocim, Bojador) finds that vinifying in concrete helps to attain purity at scale; Esporão’s new Colheita range is a case in point.
Dynamic winemaking couple Cartarina Veira and Pedro Ribeiro represent the second wave of modernists, with one foot planted in tradition.
Founded in 2000, the 70ha organically cultivated Vidigueira estate is home to a state-of-the-art winery and a beautifully renovated traditional talha winery.
Clay-made wines, Alicante Bouschet and Antão Vaz are particular strengths.

Herdade do Rocim not only has two talha cellars (one ancestral and one modern) but now organises the annual Amphora Wine Day, where producers from all over Portugal, and beyond, show their amphora-fermented and aged wines.
Arriving with a bang, Herdade do Rocim was founded in 2000 by entrepreneur José Ribeiro Vieira of Movicortes Group.

Built in 2007, the arresting modern winery in Alentejo’s Vidigueira sub-region made waves, as did the maiden release, Grande Rocim Alicante Bouschet 2007, a statement red made by José’s daughter Catarina Vieira, with consultancy from António Ventura.

Dona Maria Wines.zin: The classy range of wines produced by Júlio Bastos betrays his roots.
As for his accomplished use of Bordeaux varieties (and French oak), the Estremoz-based producer had a partnership (Quinta do Carmo) with Domaines Barons de Rothschild.

Mouchão.zin: He is a descendant of Mouchão’s John Reynolds, hence Alicante Bouschet’s star billing.

Fita Preta.zin: Co-founded in 2004 by winemaker António Maçanita and David Booth, the late viticulturist after whom the flagship red is named.

Villa Oeiras.zin: It planted a new 5.5ha vineyard in 1983 and subsequently partnered up with the municipality of Oeiras, which created the Villa Oeiras (formerly Conde de Oeiras) brand in 2009 to re-commence the production of Carcavelos on a commercial scale.

With an impeccable pedigree, Villa Oeiras wines are sourced from and vinified at estates that belonged to the Marquês de Pombal and complete their ageing in the splendour of his palatial Baroque cellar, which is open to the public by appointment.
Now with 19ha of vineyard, Villa Oeiras is easily Carcavelos’ biggest player.

Quinta da Corrieira.zin: In 2021, the region was extended to northern Oeiras to include Quinta da Corrieira, paving the way for the 2024 launch of Quinta da Corrieira Colheita 2012, the first Carcavelos wine in more than 20 years to have been produced by a private estate, such is its rarity.

Howards Folly.zin: Thus far Howards Folly have released a 1991 and 1995 Colheita, in each case back-blending a splash of wine from the following year.

Adega Belém.zin: Keen to explore different styles of Carcavelos, Adega Belém’s early 500-bottle release aged for the minimum period.

José Maria da Fonseca.zin: Owned by the Soares Franco family since the 1820s, José Maria da Fonseca is Portugal’s oldest, most venerable producer of Moscatel de Setúbal, Portugal’s other world-class fortified wine.

Quinta do Mouro.zin: Grown at 400m elevation on lean, schist soils, Quinta do Mouro and, especially Quinta do Mouro Rótulo Dourado (‘Gold Label’, launched in 2000), are well-structured, long-lived and complex.

Quinta da Fonte Souto.zin: Compared with those I tasted from Altas Quintas a decade ago, Quinta da Fonte Souto reds are especially much more sophisticated.

Herdade do Mouchão.zin: Herdade do Mouchão introduced Alentejo to its most structured variety, Alicante Bouschet and, for over a century, it has been foot-trodden and whole-bunch fermented in lagares, then aged in old 5,000-litre Portuguese oak barrels ( tonels ).

Quinta do Francês.zin: As for retail, Tanners Wine Merchants has already placed a second order for Quinta do Francês, whose range Emma Pook (author of Tanners Wines Blog) discovered on a family holiday last year.
Meanwhile, at Quinta do Francês, where the schist is ‘very old and very friable with a lot of iron and manganese,’ Patrick Agostini’s structural, intense reds have a ferrous tang.
Located in the schistous foothills of Montchique, this pioneering quality-focused estate was acquired in 2001 by Patrick Agostini (a pathologist-cum-winemaker) and his Portuguese wife, Fátima.

Casa Santos Lima.zin: First, Lisbon -based Casa Santos Lima in 2013, whose burgeoning, broad-appeal range makes it the Algarve’s top exporter.
The Lisbon-based family-owned operation, Casa Santos Lima, is one of Portugal’s top three exporters.
Since acquiring its first Algarve vineyard in Tavira in 2013, it has also become Algarve’s top exporter.
Planted primarily to leading Portuguese and French grapes, with some Negra Mole, the range has Casa Santos Lima’s trademark ‘international’ appeal and high quality-to-price ratio.

Herdade Barranco do Vale.zin: In the rugged uplands, Ana Matias Chaves’ ‘little schist mountain’ at Herdade Barranco do Vale produces firmly structured whites and reds.
Located in the schistous uplands at 100m-400m, the Algarve’s northernmost vineyard is farmed alongside cork oak, carob and almond trees.
Originally planted to red grapes by her grandfather, Ana Matias Chaves added her first white grapes in 2017 – leading Portuguese and French varieties, which share the reds’ firm acid backbone.

Falésia.zin: The once heavily planted coastal strip is typified by sand or mixed sand and clay, but it was Falésia’s propitious clifftop calcareous/black volcanic soil that encouraged Iain and Feann Brown to plant vines at Quinta dos Castanhos.

Cabrita.zin: Capturing the prevailing pale-red style, Maçanita’s colleague at Cabrita, Duarte Rito, describes it as ‘not for tourists, but what our grandfathers made and drank all year round – never with oak and as pure as could be – a low-alcohol, easygoing red.’
Exploring Negra Mole’s potential, Cabrita also makes a superb sparkling white and rosé; it has also been planted to different soils and exposures.

Alagoa Velha.zin: Young gun Carlos Raposo consults for Alagoa Velha and makes a spicy Negra Mole under his World Wild Wines label.

Following replanting in 2017, the duo are producing balanced, structured clay-aged wines that reflect the strong tempering influence of the ocean (3km away) and the Guadiana river – as well as the schist soils.

Monte da Casteleja.zin: Favouring traditional varieties and methods – the vineyard has been certified organic since 2008 – his characterful range includes a vibrant skin-contact white.

Ramilo.zin: Departing from tradition (hence the Lisboa Vinho Regional classification), Ramilo’s pioneering rosé is vinified from 300kg of its 2,000kg haul of the rare red Ramisco grape.

Dirler-Cadé.zin: Jean Dirler of Dirler-Cadé is more enthusiastic, though, noting that it excels most in top vintages and that its wines are citric and not especially powerful.

Emile Beyer.zin: Christian Beyer of Emile Beyer says that Eichberg Rieslings have good acidity and salinity, but also ample body and elegance.

Josmeyer.zin: Another biodynamic producer, Josmeyer, also makes fine Riesling from Brand.

Trimbach.zin: This 1.67ha parcel has been in the Trimbach family for more than two centuries, and many vines date from 1953 or earlier.
According to Jean Trimbach: ‘Geisberg has breadth on the palate but becomes more mineral with bottle-age.’

Bott-Geyl.zin: For Schoenenbourg, Jean-Christophe Bott of Bott-Geyl explains: ‘The main soil is marl, but it’s geologically complex.

Brigaldara.zin: Cautious about declaring blanket success, Antonio Cesari at Brigaldara describes 2016 as ‘a year for growers and terroir’.

Roccolo Grassi.zin: In the words of Marco Sartori, owner-winemaker at the Roccolo Grassi estate, ‘It was not a classic vintage’.

Tedeschi.zin: Recchia, Begali and Tedeschi’s Ansari lean towards the former, while Montresor, Pasqua and Cà La Bionda are in the more modern style.
There were those from Speri, Tedeschi and Tommasi – deeply coloured, firmly structured, with more grip to the tannins and with darker flavours and aromas.

Bertani.zin: But Bertani’s Amarone Classico is different, well known for its elegance, freshness and drinkability.

And there are technical reasons for that: since the foundation of the estate in Quinto di Valpantena, the Bertani brothers put to use what they had learned about viticulture and winemaking from the legendary French expert, Jules Guyot.
Andrea Lonardi, managing director of the Bertani group, underlines that ‘Amarone is one of the only wines affected by weather conditions after the harvest.
Between 70,000 and 110,000 bottles are produced each year at Bertani, of which 10-15% are retained to replenish the library stocks for the future.
In 2023, Bertani is due to release the 2013 vintage but then it will be necessary to wait until 2025 to buy the estate’s next new wine, as they did not produce Amarone in 2014 (nor in 2020).
By 1870, Bertani was being awarded top medals at various wine shows, and by 1880, the wine was exported around the world.
So atypical was this dry style that Bertani’s techniques were showcased at an Italian symposium in 1889.
At that time, Lonardi explained: ‘Bertani – both a grower and négociant – made white and red wines.

This cru (along with another, called ‘Le Miniere’) reflects Bertani’s desire to showcase the region’s terroir, and the audience’s positive reaction to the wine would indicate that it clearly has a place in the market.

The final three wines were the stars of the show: three vintages of Bertani’s Amarone della Valpolicella Classico, each consisting of similar blends of the local grapes and being matured for over eight years in Slavonian oak.

By law, the grapes can be dried in humidity-controlled facilities scattered around the region, but at Bertani they are dried as they were 160 years ago, in drying rooms (​​‘ fruttai ’) on the property, on bamboo racks, with the windows open to the elements.
Only made in the best years, Bertani’s Amarones have changed little, even with a change of ownership in 2011.

Serego Alighieri.zin: This vineyard selection comes from the estate of Serego Alighieri at Sant’Ambrogio, which Masi has managed since 1973.

Romano Dal Forno.zin: Romano Dal Forno’s eponymous winery deserves more recognition within the collectors’ community, as he produces some of the most mind-bending, beautiful wines anywhere in the world.
Romano Dal Forno’s earliest vintages are really interesting, as you can almost envisage him dialling everything in as he learns.

Romano Dal Forno’s Amarone is sourced from a single vineyard in the Illasi Valley, called Monte Lodoletta, located at an altitude of around 300 metres on the flatter mid-slope, overlooked by the modern winery (completed at the end of 2007).

Venturini.zin: For example, I found Venturini’s Riserva 2001 to be showing beautifully now, while some 2011s were already looking tired.

Buglioni.zin: Buglioni’s 44 Verticale Classico Superiore 2019 is a good example.

Williams Selyem.zin: In addition, names like Cobb, Peay and Williams Selyem have long been spreading the word about what this region can achieve.

Read Holland.zin: ‘My sourcing for Read Holland,’ says winemaker Ashley Holland, ‘focuses on the Deep End.

Littorai.zin: Ted Lemon of Littorai called it a ‘head-scratcher’ one that, in the end, has produced brilliant, beautiful wines from the Sonoma Coast.

Grange Saint-Sauveur.zin: ‘People expect high-volume, standardised wine from Anjou,’ says winemaker Antoine Pouponneau of Grange Saint-Sauveur, who opts to produce his (excellent) Anjou wines under the humble Vin de France label.

Domaine des Roches Neuves.zin: Comparing the styles of Chenin from these two terroirs, Thierry Germain of Domaine des Roches Neuves in Saumur, says: ‘The wines are worlds apart; it’s almost like tasting two separate varieties.’
Thierry Germain, of Domaine des Roches Neuves in Saumur-Champigny, says the 2023 vintage has produced ‘the flesh of 2022, with the finesse of 2021 and fine tannins’.

Domaine du Closel.zin: Evelyne de Pontbriand, owner of Domaine du Closel and president of the Savennières appellation, explains: ‘Until 10 years ago, we all harvested the grapes late, with botrytis – just like the sweet Chenins.

Domaine du Collier.zin: Growers such as Germain, Arnaud Lambert, Antoine Foucault (of Domaine du Collier) and Romain Guiberteau are producing consistently fine Chenins with the precision and chalky density that derive from these limestone-based soils.

Domaine Vacheron.zin: Biodynamic producer Jean-Laurent Vacheron of Domaine Vacheron says, ‘We’ve never spent so much money for so little harvest.
Domaine Vacheron, a family winery that goes back four generations, was an early adopter of bottling terroir-specific wines.

Clos Rougeard.zin: The wines of Clos Rougeard used to be made in the cramped cellars under the family house in Chacé, until the brothers found a new site nearby in 2010, with 1km of underground cellars.
Construction has been continuing between winemaking seasons, but from 2022, Clos Rougeard wines will be made in a new gravity-fed winery, equipped with 17 new concrete fermenters, holding 60hl-70hl.
The style of Clos Rougeard, ‘has to be ripe, but it has to have freshness on the palate at the same time,’ says Toublanc.
Clos Rougeard has always been a truly exceptional estate in the Saumur-Champigny appellation of the Loire.
Clos Rougeard’s Brezé white has become a cult wine, but another rarity is the Côteau de Saumur sweet wine, only produced in exceptional vintages such as 2018.

Domaine Huet.zin: An exclusive report on Domaine Huet's latest releases, plus tasting notes on several older vintages from this legendary Vouvray estate...
Founded in the Loire village of Vouvray in 1928, Domaine Huet is revered for its ageworthy Chenin Blancs.
Sarah Hwang, of Domaine Huet in Vouvray, reports a similarly long and complicated harvest, with 2023 taking twice as long as 2022.

Paul Prieur & Fils.zin: Luc Prieur of Domaine Paul Prieur & Fils notes the ‘significant difference between those vineyards facing south and those which have a southeast or easterly exposition’.

Anthony & David Girard.zin: David Girard of Domaine Anthony & David Girard agrees: ‘The slope of Les Monts Damnés starts on Kimmeridgian and finishes with Portlandian/Kimmeridgian at the top – this diversity, and the exposition of the hill, makes Les Monts Damnés very rich and varied.’

Gérard Boulay.zin: Gérard Boulay is another famous producer, whose family have been cultivating wines in Chavignol since 1310.

Didier Dagueneau.zin: Another famous, and important, name is Domaine Didier Dagueneau, perhaps the most sought-after producer of groundbreaking Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé wines.
After the untimely death of Didier Dagueneau in 2008, his son Louis-Benjamin has taken the domaine forward without losing sight of any of the principles of his father.

Henri Bourgeois.zin: Much of the credit for putting Chavignol on the map must go to Henri Bourgeois, who was working with about 2ha in the 1950s, but it is a new generation that is pushing the boundaries further.
Arnaud Bourgeois, of Domaine Henri Bourgeois (pictured, below), says: ‘In Sancerre, we have no interest in the variety.
At Henri Bourgeois, the library of wines shows conclusively that Sancerre can age deliciously for 30 years or more.
The 2020 Les Ruchons from Henri Bourgeois was one of Beverley Blanning MW’s favourites in her exploration of Sancerre’s revival.

Hubert Brochard.zin: Hubert Brochard is one of the key family domaines, with a history dating back to 1900.

In 2022, Hubert Brochard was acquired by the Bollinger group, adding another string to the bow of Bollinger’s Loire operations, which include the sparkling wines of Maison Langlois (purchased in 1973) and Château de Thauvenay in Sancerre (2016).
I have little doubt that Hubert Brochard will continue to be a benchmark producer of white, red and rosé Sancerre for many years to come.
Hubert Brochard is one of the largest landowners in Sancerre, with 60ha: 45ha planted to Sauvignon Blanc, 15ha to Pinot Noir.

Domaine de la Butte.zin: The red grapes from Domaine de la Butte are totally destemmed, and both red and white grapes are thoroughly sorted on tables to ensure only the best grapes are used.

Domaine de la Taille aux Loups.zin: Jacky Blot (Domaine de la Taille aux Loups, Montlouis) is convinced that 2019 is a great vintage for white wines, and is much better than 2018.
Jacky Blot of Domaine de la Taille aux Loups had a similar experience: ‘We were down 50% at 19hL/ha but the quality was a nice surprise with good mature grapes.’

Domaine Belargus.zin: Ivan Massonnat of Domaine Belargus in Anjou said: ‘From the end of March to the beginning of April, our team spent precisely 15 nights standing, fighting alongside our vines.
Domaine Belargus declares that 2023 was the rainiest harvest in the area for 10 years.

Famille Bourgeois.zin: Jean-Marie Bourgeois, of Famille Bourgeois confirmed, ‘We haven’t made our top cuvées, like Jadis, in 2021.’

Domaine du Mortier.zin: Domaine du Mortier was particularly successful in this respect, with three of its wines from both Bourgueil and St-Nicolas de Bourgueil being placed in the top 12.

Domaine Yannick Amirault.zin: These are the words of Benoît Amirault, of Domaine Yannick Amirault in Bourgueil.

Domaine des Sables Verts.zin: Hervé Malinge, of Domaine des Sables Verts in Saumur-Champigny, comments, ‘It was a very challenging vintage.

Domaine de la Noblaie.zin: Chinon-based Jérôme Billard, of Domaine de la Noblaie says, ‘The biggest challenge now is the climate; everything else we can manage.’

François et Julien Pinon.zin: Julien Pinon, of François et Julien Pinon, says, ‘grey rot is a fungus, but acid rot is caused by a bacteria that turns wine into vinegar.

Frédéric Mabileau.zin: Seek out Frédéric Mabileau’s Chenin du Puy, Saumur 2016, which is lean and austere, but has a richness and ripeness to the fruit which brings balance.

Mélaric.zin: Another top pick from Saumur is Mélaric, Billes de Roche, Saumur 2018, which is elegant and precise.

Domaine des Forges.zin: A top bottle to try is Domaine des Forges, Quarts de Chaume Grand Cru 2014 which has a rich and heady scent of grilled honeyed peaches, apricot and frangipane tart.

Cave Verdier-Logel.zin: Cave Verdier-Logel has some of its vines here, on the steep slopes.
Cave Verdier-Logel – the first serious independent producer here when the local cooperative was virtually the only producer in the area.

Gilles Bonnefoy.zin: Gilles Bonnefoy in the Côtes du Forez has some vines at 600m, while Domaine Sérol (Côte Roannaise) has a parcel at 500m.

Domaine des Bérioles.zin: Domaine des Bérioles – run by Jean Teissèdre, sister Sophie Roux and her husband Jérôme, this organic domaine is one of the best in the Upper Loire.

Domaine Grosbot-Barbara.zin: Domaine Grosbot-Barbara – Denis Barbara, the loose-limbed rock star of St-Pourçain, had the vision and determination to create the beautiful vineyard of Mont-Georges.

Domaine des Pothiers.zin: Domaine des Pothiers – now run by the dynamic Romain Paire who makes fine organic and biodynamic Côte Roannaise wines, including Riesling.

Famille Lieubeau.zin: There were early April frosts here, as François Lieubeau, of Famille Lieubeau, explains: ‘Four nights of frost from 31 March to 4 April, with temperatures below -3.5C, once again kept us on our toes.’

Domaine Brégeon.zin: Lailler, winemaker and owner of Domaine Brégeon, explains that the wines are born from a subsoil of gabbro, a dense, dark and impenetrable igneous rock.

Jérémie Huchet.zin: This might be an extreme view, but certainly there are other winemakers, such as Jérémie Huchet, who are unconvinced that batonnage works for their terroir and style: ‘It erases the terroir,’ he says.

Vincent Pinard.zin: The 2019 domaine Sancerre from Vincent Pinard shows that is possible to have ripe fruit, sufficient concentration as well as finesse and delicacy.
Florent Pinard (Domaine Vincent Pinard, Sancerre) recalls: ‘We harvested the 2020 vintage on 28 August.
This was confirmed by Florent Pinard, of the Vincent Pinard domaine in Sancerre: ‘For both our whites and reds we had to select the grapes we used very carefully.

Domaine de la Pépière.zin: Since then, a number of leading producers – including Jo Landron, Vincent Caillé, Domaine Luneau-Papin and Domaine de la Pépière – have forged a distinct identity for their wines, and overall quality has increased immensely.

Domaine Ménard-Gaborit.zin: Yields were down 60% at Famille Lieubeau and 80% at Domaine Ménard-Gaborit – a bitter pill to swallow for 30-year-olds François Ménard and his wife Pauline, who took over the family domaine in 2021.

Château de Passavant.zin: Château de Passavant gets less media attention than some more high-profile Loire Chenin producers, so it is good to see its 2014 Jarret de Monchenin emerging as our only Outstanding wine.

Baudry-Dutour.zin: In Chinon, Jean-Martin Dutour of Baudry-Dutour said: ‘Despite the small crop we are very happy with the reds; due to the fine September our Cabernet Franc reached 12.5% alcohol and was phenolically ripe.’

Domaine FL.zin: Domaine FL’s Savennières Roche-aux- Moines 2016 supports my conviction that if I could only drink a single style of wine for the rest of my life it would have to be Loire Chenin Blanc.

Château de Beaucastel.zin: In the Rhône, Château de Beaucastel is going strong, especially the Mourvèdre-dominant Hommage à Jacques Perrin, if you can find it.
It was the same figure at Château de Beaucastel, where César Perrin agrees on the importance of old vines.
‘We are no longer in the era of extraction,’ says François Perrin of Château de Beaucastel; ‘we’re in the era of elegance – but our elegance.’
Along with Mourvèdre, César Perrin at Château de Beaucastel was particularly pleased with the quality of the Roussanne in Châteauneuf-du-Pape.
In Châteauneuf-du-Pape, Château de Beaucastel was successful, and Mas Saint Louis shows the aromatic, peppery style of the vintage.
The best wines of Châteauneuf such as Château de Beaucastel’s ‘Hommage à Jacques Perrin’ are deliciously harmonious now, and will continue to age well for another decade, if not more.

Château Rayas.zin: Despite its arcane reputation, Château Rayas is not an old estate in the context of Châteauneuf-du-Pape.
Château Rayas is indeed a Châteauneuf, but it bears little resemblance to other wines made in the appellation.
Château Rayas makes a richly textured white Châteauneuf from 50% Clairette, 50% Grenache Blanc.

Château de Fonsalette.zin: Rayas, Pignan and Château de Fonsalette are all made at Rayas; any barrels deemed unsuitable for these cuvées are blended together to make La Pialade.

Domaine de la Vieille Julienne.zin: Antoine Daumen of Domaine de la Vieille Julienne was unsure about the season as it progressed.
Some winemakers I spoke to, such as Jean-Paul Daumen of Domaine de la Vieille Julienne and Jean-Louis Chave, believe this is evidence of vines adapting to an increasingly extreme climate.
Jean-Paul Daumen of Domaine de la Vieille Julienne said ‘I can’t compare it to any other vintage – it’s like a UFO.’

Domaine Le Sang des Cailloux.zin: Frédéri Férigoule of Domaine Le Sang des Cailloux stressed the importance of green harvesting in 2022: ‘We had a good crop load, but it was too much to ripen,’ he says.

Domaine des Bosquets.zin: A standout producer this year is Julien Brechet of Domaine des Bosquets and he describes 2024 as ‘a very honest vintage,’ meaning that it’s highly expressive of terroir, detailed and precise.
Reds are particularly fine, well-balanced and harmonious now; Domaine des Bosquets and Château Rayas were both in a particularly satisfying state of maturity last year.

Clos du Mont-Olivet.zin: Châteauneuf-du-Pape, particularly the heavily Grenache-based wines from Clos du Mont-Olivet, Marcoux and Rayas, was perhaps the easiest to recognise with the pale hue, sweet fruit and structure.
The Châteauneuf-du-Pape wines all retail at more than €50, except for Clos du Mont-Olivet, while Château Rayas is around €700-a-bottle and Beaucastel Hommage à Jacques Perrin at €480.

Domaine de la Janasse.zin: That being said we were all on song for, respectively, the Domaine de la Janasse and Tardieu-Laurent Vieilles Vignes, as well as Domaine Peyre Rose (a top scoring wine in 2019 as well), but missed the reserved presence of Château de Beaucastel’s Hommage à Jacques Perrin.

Château de Montfaucon.zin: Rodolphe des Pins of Château de Montfaucon says ‘it’s a great vintage – I was a bit surprised, I thought it would be more unbalanced.’

Domaine Font de Michelle.zin: Guillaume Gonnet of Domaine Font de Michelle and his own eponymous label says: ‘In 10 years I haven’t planted any Grenache,’ instead replanting Mourvèdre, Counoise, Clairette and Bourboulenc.

Clos des Papes.zin: In the words of Vincent Avril of Clos des Papes, ‘it’s just nature – there is no explanation.’
‘It happened in one night,’ says Vincent Avril of Clos des Papes who eventually lost 70% of his crop.
And Vincent Avril of Clos des Papes was impressed by the Bourboulenc and Piquepoul Blanc.

Moulin de la Gardette.zin: In the south, Gigondas fared well (for producers such as Moulin de la Gardette, Domaine Les Semelles de Vent, and Mas des Restanques); some Châteauneufs were also very good (from Clos des Papes, Rotem & Mounir Saouma, and Henri Bonneau ).

Domaine Juliette Avril.zin: An estate that’s been going from strength to strength over the past five years, Domaine Juliette Avril made some excellent red Châteauneufs in 2024, from its tradition bottling all the way up to its cuvées spéciales.

Domaine Lombard.zin: And a Domaine Lombard Brézème blanc 2008 tasted recently was a revelation, brimming with citrusy acidity, lavender honey and violets: a wine of extraordinary character.

Mas de Boislauzon.zin: In Châteauneuf, all the wines of Mas de Boislauzon are in a good place, as is Clos des Papes.

Domaine Chamfort.zin: Aside from that, ‘2020 was a fairly easy year,’ says Vasco Perdigao of Domaine Chamfort, ‘even if “easy” years don’t really exist!’

Domaine Notre Dame des Pallières.zin: Isabelle Roux of Domaine Notre Dame des Pallières says that a light touch in the cellar was the key to success, ‘with light extractions in order to preserve this fruit, this freshness and this finesse which brings us so much happiness when tasting them today,’ she says.

Domaine de Beaurenard.zin: Frédéric Coulon of Domaine de Beaurenard says that ‘2020 is a beautiful vintage that we like a lot in the family, because it has good ripeness, good balance with sufficient acidity, fine tannins, good length and a beautiful aromatic expression.’

Domaine Raspail-Ay.zin: In comparison the Domaine Raspail-Ay is comfortably mature and drinking beautifully.

Domaine Brusset.zin: Domaine Brusset’s Les Hauts de Montmirail was excellent, however.

Domaine du Pesquier.zin: Both 1999s – Domaine du Pesquier, and Pierre Amadieu’s Domaine Grande Romane – had the vibrancy and straightness of this vintage and were alive and tense.

Pierre Amadieu.zin: Pierre Amadieu explains that it was an underrated year, characterised by its ‘extremely clean fruit, contrasting with the big and powerful 1998’.

Domaine Saint Gayan.zin: The 1998 Domaine Saint Gayan was particularly enjoyable, however; a wine to sink into like an old leather armchair.

Domaine Les Goubert.zin: Domaine Les Goubert’s Cuvée Florence and the ever-dependable Domaine Santa Duc’s Les Hautes Garrigues were both show-stoppers.

Domaine du Cayron.zin: ‘One of my favourite vintages,’ says Delphine Faraud of Domaine du Cayron, who counts 1985, 1978 and 1971 as exceptional older years.

Château La Nerthe.zin: Châteauneuf-du-Pape takes two spots in the list, one red and one white, and although one is an older vintage (Château La Nerthe’s 1999 Cadettes), if you have it in your cellar, its 98-point score suggests now is the time to drink it.

Château Latour.zin: In 1996, Château Latour was under the third year of owner François Pinault, and the second year with Frédéric Engerer as commercial director, before he went on to become CEO of the First Growth in 1998.

Helène Genin, technical director at Château Latour, explained how the estate used a triple-row sorting table for the first time ever to remove lesser grapes with the utmost care, whether mildew affected, sunburnt or underripe.

Château Lafleur.zin: Commenting on Bordeaux 2018, Château Lafleur estate manager Omri Ram says, ‘It would not have been easy to make great wine in this crazy kind of season even a decade ago – with the vines receiving an excess of water at first, then the valve being abruptly turned off.
Château Lafleur has held up well and shows gorgeously seductive, if subtle, notes of truffle and undergrowth.

Château Mouton Rothschild.zin: One wine that Jane Anson highlighted in this year’s En Primeur coverage was Château Mouton Rothschild, Le Petit Mouton, which she described as ‘very moreish’ and said ‘there are not many 2nd wines that can truly stand on their own but this is very much one of them’.

Château Margaux.zin: Philippe Bascaules at Château Margaux recorded less dehyrdration in the grapes in 2020 compared to 2018; so high alcohols were avoided, and a more classic balance is found in the wines.’
Philippe Bascaules at Château Margaux recorded less dehyrdration in the grapes in 2020 compared to 2018; so high alcohols were avoided, and a more classic balance is found in the wines.
Over at Château Margaux, 2020 is the 100th anniversary of the white wine bottled under the name Pavillon Blanc (although there has been a white wine here for 300 years).

At Château Margaux, estate director Philippe Bascaules said that 10% of the harvest was lost due to sunburnt grapes, with the heat so unbearable some days in late August that harvesters had to stop working at 10am.
With regards tannins, Château Margaux’s grand vin has an IPT (Total Polyphenol Index) of 63 which is ‘more like the 1996 vintage,’ winemaker Philippe Bascaules noted.
Of the five first growths in the era, only Château Margaux still has the same person in charge today, with Corinne Mentzelopoulos taking over in 1980.

While it would be churlish to suggest that the late Paul Pontallier (pictured) of Château Margaux 2011, 2012, 2013 and 2014 were all ‘difficult vintages’, they were certainly less lauded than the two vintages that preceded them.
Château Margaux – 2015 the last vintage under the late, great Paul Pontallier – is the best of the firsts, while on the Right Bank, Château Lafleur is the wine of the vintage.
I will not contest that point, but I would argue that both Château Cheval Blanc and Château Margaux 1985 have evolved to a point that they rival many of the legendary wines of the last half-century.
My highlighted wines include Palmer, d’Issan and Rauzan-Ségla, while Château Margaux itself was also a notable success across all three of its wines.

Château Cheval Blanc.zin: However, they’re likely to be harder to come by on the open market and, as an example, the 100pt Château Cheval Blanc 1990, if you can find it, is likely to fetch near £1,000 per bottle.

Château Brown.zin: In Pessac-Léognan and the Graves, the Sauvignon Blancs handled the heat wave better than the Sémillons, which explains why many wines, from Château Brown Blanc to La Mission Haut-Brion Blanc, have higher-than-normal percentages of Sauvignon Blanc in the blends.

Château du Tertre.zin: There are new owners at Château du Tertre (the Helfrich family), and at Tour de Mons (Nathalie Perrodo, as at Marquis d’Alesme).

Château Rauzan-Ségla.zin: Nearby Château Rauzan-Ségla, also under organic management, had a yield of 30hl/ha.
Overall, the 2013s are only slightly cheaper than the superior 2012s and 2014s, though Château Rauzan-Ségla, to its credit, did cut its release price by a third.

Château Lascombes.zin: For Axel Heinz, ex-Ornellaia winemaker and now the director of Château Lascombes, the 2024 ‘took a lot of energy – it wasn’t the easiest but it was far from a disaster’.

Château La Lagune.zin: At 94 points we have Château La Lagune, performing brilliantly in this vintage.

Château Cantemerle.zin: For the classified wines in these appellations, La Lagune is in its final year of biodynamic conversion, and there are changes at Château Cantemerle with Philippe Dambrine stepping down to be replaced by Laure Canu as estate director (who was previously at Château Angélus).

Château d’Agassac.zin: Château d’Agassac was bought by Gérard Jicquel (who also bought Fourcas Dupré last year).

Château Lanessan.zin: Château Lanessan 2020 is the last vintage with Paz Espejo – shame, as she has done a great job at this property.
