Château Batailley.zin: The good news is that mid-range classified brands succeeded too, including fine performances from Château Batailley, Château Clerc-Milon, Château Duhart Milon, Château Haut-Bages Libéral and Château Pedesclaux, for example.

Clos Fourtet.zin: Estates on limestone; Belair Monange, the two Beausejours and Clos Fourtet did extremely well not to lean too heavily into austerity while Figeac and Cheval produced really lovely wines in 2024.

Château Montrose.zin: Château Montrose and Château Cos d’Estournel were my top picks, with both bottles upgraded by a point from their En Primeur score.
Château Cos d’Estournel and Château Montrose proved the two best from the appellation but the edge goes to Château Montrose, for which only 35% of the harvest was used.
Top wines: Château Cos d’Estournel and Château Montrose proved the two best from the appellation, but the edge goes to Château Montrose, for which only 35% of the harvest was used.

Château Lafon-Rochet.zin: Château Lafon-Rochet (the first full vintage with ex-Lafite winemaker Christophe Congé in charge) and Château Le Boscq are both fantastic.

Château de Pez.zin: Château de Pez is one estate that shines brightly among the 2023 wines.

Château Beychevelle.zin: Château Beychevelle for example, had its highest proportion ever of Cabernet Sauvignon, according to the estate.

Château Ducru-Beaucaillou.zin: For Bruno Borie, owner of Château Ducru-Beaucaillou, he is ‘pretty proud’ of what they have made in 2024.

Château Lagrange.zin: Château Lagrange (the St-Julien, one) used the same technique despite 2024 being its ‘lowest ever yield’, at 26hl/ha, said director Matthieu Bordes.

Château Léoville Barton.zin: For Damien Barton Sartorius, owner and general manager of Château Léoville Barton, the 2024 vintage was all about ‘hard work’.

Domaine de Chevalier.zin: Hard to find any wines to recommend today, although I tasted a Domaine de Chevalier white two years ago (out of magnum) that was delivering a lovely push and pull of truffle and saffron.

Château Sociando-Mallet.zin: I strongly recommend Château Sociando-Mallet Haut-Médoc for a wine that shows you don’t have to buy classified estates to still get quality at 25 years old.

Château Dauzac.zin: NB: Château Dauzac 2008 was tasted at the estate in Bordeaux.

Château Smith Haut Lafitte.zin: Château Smith Haut Lafitte in Pessac-Léognan hired 200 sorters, but few other estates could emulate them, especially since demand for pickers was intense.

Château Lafite Rothschild.zin: Carruades de Lafite, the second wine of Château Lafite Rothschild, was released 6% below its 2020-vintage en primeur price on an ex-Bordeaux basis (€ per bottle), with Pavie down 2.5%, Château Batailley flat year-on-year and Château Cheval Blanc up 3%.
More recently, both Château Lafite Rothschild and Château Margaux have been fabulous, even with some ullage (the wine level reduced in the neck or shoulder of the bottle).

Château Palmer.zin: Château Palmer, one of the wines of the appellation, had plenty of excellent Merlot and proved more balanced and refined, all the while exhibiting rare opulence, compared to its 2022 vintage.

Moreover, we are looking here at Château Palmer wines over five-year intervals, covering the Palmer 2015, 2010, 2005, 2000, 1995 and 1990 vintages, which neatly showcases the impact of ageing on a classified Margaux.

Château Talbot.zin: Although Château Talbot is not the most prestigious property in St-Julien – that likely goes to Château Léoville Las Cases – Château Talbot is as characteristic of St-Julien as St-Julien is to Bordeaux.
Château Talbot, classified as a 4th growth in the Médoc Classification of 1855, is one of St-Julien’s largest estates, encompassing about 110ha, in one single block around the estate.
Château Talbot frequently flies under the radar and fails to receive the accolades it deserves, perhaps because it is such a large estate with such a large production.
As you’ll see from the tasting notes below, the wines of Château Talbot have become more refined and polished over the last two decades.

Clos des Lunes.zin: In his Clos des Lunes range, Olivier Bernard, owner of Domaine de Chevalier and Château Lespault-Martillac in Pessac-Léognan, produces three dry whites based on different blends, ageing methods and soil types.

Château Haut-Bailly.zin: Château Haut-Bailly has made one of its greatest wines from the Bordeaux 2015 vintage, says Jane Anson as part of her review of Pessac-Léognan 2015 red wines in-bottle.

Château Le Coteau.zin: In terms of wines to seek out that you may not have had before, I particularly enjoyed Château Le Coteau and the ‘Margaux’ appellation wine from Maison Sichel.

Château La Mission Haut-Brion.zin: Château Haut-Brion and Château La Mission Haut-Brion were both impressive, with the former presenting an almost understated expression, it was more relaxed and open compared to LMHB at this point.

Petrus.zin: For Olivier Berrout at Petrus the quick harvest was crucial, ‘we couldn’t wait 24 hours once we started to get good maturity,’ as well as the overall balance.
Petrus is understandably the standard bearer, producing a wine that many believe has surpassed those produced at this address in both 1961 and 1945, the two most iconic vintages of the century.

Château La Conseillante.zin: My standout was Château La Conseillante which was not only one of the best I’ve tasted from this estate, but also one of the most vibrant and joyful at this stage.

Vieux Château Certan.zin: Vieux Château Certan was absolutely sublime with an effortless elegance – I have high hopes for the future of this wine as well as L’Eglise-Clinet that is complex and characterful.
The second wine of VCC, La Gravette de Vieux Château Certan is also a stellar wine and much more like a baby grand vin than a second wine.

Clos du Clocher.zin: Clos du Clocher, Seraphine, Clinet and Guillot Clauzel are also well worth seeking out.

Occhipinti.zin: Encouraged by her uncle, Giusto Occhipinti, who had co-founded the renowned COS estate, she established a garage winery, relying on rudimentary equipment and embracing a minimalist philosophy from day one.

By making some of the brightest and juiciest wines in Italy, Arianna Occhipinti’s success stems, in part, from her unique ability to defy the stereotypes that Sicilian reds are simply hearty and jammy.
Arianna Occhipinti’s wines have become increasingly refined and focused over time.

Ata Rangi.zin: Ata Rangi first achieved full organic certification for two of its vineyards, McCrone and Home Block, in 2014, with the rest following soon after, and is also unusual in New Zealand in that a large percentage of its vines remain on their own roots.
Widely regarded as one of New Zealand’s best wineries, Ata Rangi’s stylish, complex Pinot Noirs have a solid track record for ageing beautifully.
Ata Rangi took over the vineyard in 2015, and purchased it in 2017; it was certified organic in 2018.
Wines were poured from magnums, with vintages missing from the Ata Rangi cellar kindly donated by a local collector.

Wild Irishman.zin: His much younger colleague Brian Shaw, co-owner and winemaker at Wild Irishman in Alexandra, explains how gently he now extracts.
Shaw of Wild Irishman notes: ‘Alexandra is the hottest and coldest place in New Zealand – it is very continental.’

Mount Edward.zin: Duncan Forsyth of Mount Edward sums it up when he says: ‘The way we have evolved stylistically is that these elements like tannin and acid are coming at you anyway.

Felton Road.zin: That is the story of Nigel Greening, British-born owner of Felton Road in Central Otago, New Zealand, who just celebrated his 25th vintage.
He says ‘Felton Road lives in these two halves, before and after.’
‘We have to audit for every bottle of Felton Road in the world to its final consumption.
So once again Felton Road is at the forefront of viticulture.

Greywacke.zin: Kevin was in the UK to celebrate the 10th anniversary of Greywacke, and to mark the occasion we were treated to two examples of each of the seven wines – the first vintage of each wine, and the most recent.

Casa Ferreirinha.zin: Casa Ferreirinha thus became the first house in the Douro dedicated to making a table wine, which has always come from vineyards situated at different altitudes in the Douro Superior region.
Since 2003 he has led the teams responsible for Casa Ferreirinha, Ferreira, Offley and Sandeman.
Meaning ‘House of little Ferreira’, Casa Ferreirinha has arguably outshone its parent, Ferreira Port House.
However, named after the diminutive lady (‘little Ferreira’), Casa Ferreirinha Barca Velha was originally – and for many years – made and principally sourced from Meão.
From the ‘stars-aligned’ 2011 Douro vintage, Casa Ferreirinha Barca Velha – the original icon – is a shoo-in.
In stark contrast with Sogrape’s other flagship Douro red, Casa Ferreirinha Barca Velha, Legado is not only the product of a single vineyard, it is also made every year.
First made in 1952, Casa Ferreirinha’s iconic red Barca Velha was virtually a lone voice in the wilderness.

Symington Family Estates.zin: Founded in 1999 by Symington Family Estates (SFE) and Bruno Prats, former owner of Bordeaux’s Château Cos d’Estournel, Prats & Symington is the partnership through which the prestigious Port wine dynasty successfully forged a new path.

Prats & Symington.zin: Though similarly focused on the Tourigas (with a splash of Tinta Amarela), the Prats & Symington wines made for an interesting comparison with SFE’s Douro wines from Quinta do Vesuvio, one of Chryseia’s original sources.

Portugal Boutique Winery.zin: Portugal Boutique Winery’s lighter-styled Boina Red highlighted the benefits of aged (centenarian) vines, using fast-disappearing varieties such as Gouveio-Preto, Tinta Carvalha, Alicante Bouschet and Alvarelhão.

Quinta Nova.zin: Quinta Nova’s trio of 92-pointers also showed an impressive and nuanced grip of the market.

Quinta de la Rosa.zin: Some of the properties below (such as Quinta do Noval, Quinta de la Rosa and Quinta do Vesúvio) have become shippers in their own right, producing a range of wines (both Port and Douro) as well as a Single Quinta Vintage Port nearly every year.
There really can be no finer present than Quinta de la Rosa, which was given to Claire Feuerheerd for her christening in 1906.

Sandeman.zin: Others are an important part of larger shippers such as Graham’s, Sandeman or Taylor’s, and in declared years their output contributes to their house vintage Port blends.
Seixo is now the basis for Sandeman’s much-improved vintage Ports (the 2018 looks really very promising), but it has only been bottled quite rarely as a single quinta vintage.
Luís Sottomayor, of Sandeman, Ferreira and Offley, adds: ‘The degrees of complexity, colour and structure make the 2016 wines absolutely exceptional.’

Quinta do Noval.zin: Noval’s vineyards have always been impeccably maintained and the whitewashed steps connecting one walled terrace to another are visible for miles around.

Although Noval is the house name that appears on wines coming from outside the quinta, the name ‘Quinta do Noval’ is reserved for late bottled vintage, colheita and vintage Ports, all of which originate from the property itself.
Oh, to have been a fly on the wall at the launch of Quinta do Noval Nacional Vintage Port 1931.
For Lay & Wheeler buyer Fiona Hayes, Quinta do Noval Vinha da Marka 2019 has ‘a significant USP’ which ‘needs to be conveyed to those drinking it.’
If Quinta do Noval Nacional Vintage Port is Everest, this Himalayan Douro dozen offers alternative peak drinking.
Quinta do Noval is probably the most famous Port producer in the Douro.
Any wine labelled ‘Quinta do Noval’ is made from grapes grown at the property, whereas any wine labelled simply ‘Noval’ will have been made from at least a portion of grapes that have been bought in.
In the years between 1994 and 2016, Quinta do Noval made 14 vintage declarations whereas Quinta do Noval Nacional was declared 10 times.

That terroir surely accounts for Quinta do Noval ’s history of eccentric vintage declarations, starting with the Pinhão Valley quinta’s legendary 1931 vintage, and explains why it stands out in generally declared years, such as 2000.
Established in 1715, Quinta do Noval is famous for its vintage Ports – particularly its 1.6ha of ungrafted vines used to produce icon wine Nacional.
In 2019 Quinta do Noval purchased the neighbouring Quinta do Passadouro estate, which has two main vineyard parcels in the Pinhão Valley and the Roncão Valley, totalling 36ha.
Christian Seely, managing director of Quinta do Noval, also reported on the testing conditions: ‘2022 was a year of extremes, both very hot and very dry.

Niepoort.zin: He made Niepoort’s revered 1945 Vintage Port and an everyday ‘light’ (unfortified) red wine for his workers labelled Vinho de Consumo 1938.
By the time Dirk took over from his father in 1997, Redoma Tinto Douro DOC, which Niepoort first made in 1991, had placed him at the forefront of Douro winemaking.

A recent vertical of Niepoort’s classic Douro reds (Redoma, Batuta and Charme) from the 1990s to the present day revealed a journey that has not been without its challenges, given the Douro’s extremes of heat and drought-prone climate.
While its Ports are naturally full-bodied, since 2005 or thereabouts Niepoort has excluded overripe grapes and, latterly, picked earlier.
In the old days, Niepoort’s three growers each had one vat of ‘vintage potential’ Port.
But in 2011 Niepoort had 50 vats – ‘all better than any from the past,’ says Dirk.
Dirk’s quest for ever fresher, more elegant wines has also extended the boundaries of Niepoort’s Portuguese empire beyond the Douro to more temperate climes.
Then there are the overseas collaborations behind Niepoort’s project wines – one-offs or short runs.
A link-up with Equipo Navazos in Jerez has since seen Niepoort create Ururabo, a Douro white that’s aged under flor like Sherry.

Founded in 2016 by Niepoort and Piesport winemaker Philipp Kettern, it has been home to Dirk’s Germany-based sons Daniel and Marco – though, in early 2020, Daniel (the eldest) transferred to Niepoort.
All told, Niepoort now produces around 2.2 million bottles per year, of which around 85% is wine, 15% Port.
As for Niepoort’s Douro growers, Daniel is encouraging them to cultivate vineyards sustainably – thus nurturing his love of viticulture.
For Dirk Niepoort, whose family firm declared both a classic and single quinta vintage port (SQVP), 2015 was ‘as perfect as it gets’.
For Dirk Niepoort from the eponymous Port house, 2019 was ‘not as perfect as 2017’ – which was Niepoort’s last declaration – with 2019 ‘possibly bigger but still a very elegant year.
By contrast, Niepoort Turris is aged in large foudres: wilder, and with distinct forest notes, it is a different animal altogether.

Describing them as ‘chalk and cheese,’ Hedonism’s Viner says that the single vinha wines from Crasto and Niepoort resonate with consumers’ willingness ‘to spend more to discover new things and expand their knowledge’.
While Crasto’s offerings are opulent, Niepoort’s championing of elevated sites and earlier picking produces a fresh, elegant expression which is low in alcohol.

Founded in 1842 by Franciscus Marius van der Niepoort, in 1991 his great-great-grandson Dirk Niepoort added a fresh, now equally prestigious string to the Port house’s bow, launching Redoma – Niepoort’s first Douro wine.
Niepoort says Paulson’s bottle of La Tâche 1991 prompted him to ask: ‘How is it possible that the wine is so aromatic, yet so fine?’
Niepoort is not the only producer to take inspiration from Domaine Romanée-Conti.
It is no coincidence that, bar one (Niepoort Redoma), all my recommended Portuguese white wines were first made this century.

All five producers have a longstanding family tradition of making Port, even if – with the exception of Niepoort (a sixth generation Port shipper) – it was sold to shippers who, until 1986, enjoyed a monopoly over export sales.

Both Ports were based on Niepoort’s magnificent 1863 pipa which produced a 2018 Lalique bottling (the world’s most expensive Port ever sold) and the outstanding bottling we tasted from 1992, Dirk’s eldest son’s birth year.

That intern was Dirk Niepoort, and the journey he predicted – evocative labels from Robustus (his first 1990 Douro red) to Charme (launched in 2002) – reflects not only this now fêted fifth-generation Port and winemaker’s progress, but also a region-wide direction of travel.
Chief among them is Niepoort, whose quest for freshness has seen him push the envelope hardest on earlier picking and big-format oak (foudres and vats).

At a pre-release tasting of premier 2017 Douro reds in June, Niepoort’s Batuta, Redoma and Vertente contrasted starkly with other wines that were deeply coloured and concentrated with imposing tannins.
I asked Niepoort if the pendulum has swung too far, verging on under-ripeness or under-extraction, which, as Moreira vividly puts it, ‘can steal the character of a place’.

Conceding ‘perhaps a little’, Niepoort nonetheless believes ‘we are absolutely on the right track’, because bottling the ‘perfect wine’ (such as his 2011s) does not allow for ‘growth’ in bottle, hence now ‘bottling with a bit of lightness’.

With multiple aspects and altitudes (100m to 850m above sea level) – which, observes Niepoort, differentiate the Douro from other classic regions – Douro DOC winemakers have led the way in interrogating this large region’s 42,023ha of vineyard.

Fonseca.zin: For Guimaraens, whose family firm Fonseca also celebrated its bicentenary in 2015, a classic declaration is not just about quality.

It’s rare to get back-to-back vintage declarations – for some houses you have to go back to 1934/35 (Fonseca for example) but for others, not since 1846/47 have two generally-declared Port vintages come one after the other.
Fonseca and Taylor’s already show purity of fruit and have the structure to continue to drink well for the next 20 years or so.
Going back to the 1980s, there is a caveat emptor on some of the 1985s, though Fonseca is faultless and in my opinion the leading wine of the vintage.
From 1977, Fonseca is a tower of strength with Dow’s and Graham’s 1970 both worthy of being ranked alongside the 20th-century greats.
David Guimaraens, winemaker for Taylor, Fonseca and Croft, sums it up when he says: ‘Balance is one of the keynotes of the vintage.
For Croft, having recently been acquired by Taylor Fonseca, this was the first harvest since 1963 to be foot-trodden.

Ferreira.zin: Luís Sottomayor, responsible for Ferreira, Offley and Sandeman is even more fulsome.
Luís Sottomayor from Ferreira and Sandeman describes 2019 as ‘a very good year with freshness and great balance’.

Ramos Pinto.zin: Ana Rosas of Ramos Pinto says: ‘It was one of the most challenging years for viticulture, however the wines produced are very pure with exceptional fruit.’
Ramos Pinto’s CEO Jorge Rosas is similarly taking ‘a closer zoom’ to showcase best performing parcels or blocks in top years with new Douro launch, Ramos Pinto Quinta de Ervamoira 2018.

Quinta do Crasto.zin: There has also been an increase in Douro wines – a category pioneered by Quinta do Crasto, who first produced Vinha Maria Teresa and Vinha da Ponte in 1998.
First making wine in 1994, Quinta do Crasto is based in the Cima Corgo sub-region, Port’s heartland.
Roquette showed it alongside Quinta do Crasto Colheita 1997.
Similarly (and, to maintain profile), Wine & Soul and Quinta do Crasto are using massal selection to replicate old vineyards.
Quinta do Crasto’s Maria Teresa comes from a plot of 54 grape varieties from heritage vines, according to Miguel Roquette, who says ‘the recipe is in the field’.

Wine & Soul.zin: Serôdio Borges was stunned by the intern-cum-model from Lisbon who loved this rugged, remote region of his birth.
Since 2004, several elevated, old-vine parcels in Porrais have produced Wine & Soul Guru, an exceptional Douro white, recently joined by Guru NM, an innovative non-vintage iteration.
In 2009, Wine & Soul inherited Quinta da Manoella, from which it produces an elegant red and a tawny Port.
Wine & Soul’s riper, darker, muscular Pintas is from a sunnier, south-facing site in Vale de Mendiz which, observes Moreira, integrates oak more readily.

Sogrape.zin: Antonini’s role directing Sogrape’s precision viticulture programme between 2008 and 2012 was immensely important, according to Guedes.

Quinta do Vale Meão.zin: Claiming similarly distinguished roots, cousins Francisco Ferreira (Quinta do Vallado) and Francisco Olazábal (Quinta do Vale Meão) are descended from Dona Antónia Adelaide Ferreira who, respectively, owned and established their quintas during the 19th century.
Once the Olazábal family took control of the property at Quinta do Vale Meão, they wasted no time making a Port with the extra grapes; fortuitously, 2000 was a terrific (generally declared) vintage.

At Quinta do Vale Meão, Francisco Olazabal points out, ‘tannin is something that is not lacking in most Douro varieties’, so his barrels are now ‘more neutral, with less toast, less wood sweetness and tannin’.

Quinta do Vallado.zin: Quinta do Vallado swiftly made its mark with mellifluous Tawny Ports with an indication of age (10, 20, 30 or 40-year-old) and impeccably sourced ultra-rare Very Old (19th century) Tawny Ports.

Luis Seabra.zin: Take Luis Seabra’s wines, which showcase whole-bunch ferments – another tool increasingly used to create a sense of freshness and levity, not least because, says Seabra, ‘it forces me not to extract too much’.

Folias de Baco.zin: Tiago Sampaio (Folias de Baco) has planted Pinot Noir and Tinta Francisca there for single-varietal wines, while his Uivo Renegado – a sappy 50/50, white/red old field-blend wine – reflects a niche revival of lighter-bodied ‘palhete’ or ‘clarete’ wines.

Titan of Douro.zin: From the Douro’s highest point, the granite and quartz slopes of Serra do Reboredo, Luís Leocádio (Titan of Douro) makes intensely characterful, mineral, fresh wines from un-grafted, 150-year-old vineyards planted at 700m-850m by his wife’s great grandfather.

Smith Woodhouse.zin: According to Symington, whose family firm declared Cockburn, Dow, Graham and Warre as well as Smith Woodhouse and Quinta do Vesuvio: ‘This was a year when it was vitally important to know your vineyards, which varieties to pick and when.’

Burmester.zin: Carlos Alves, winemaker for Barros, Burmester, Cálem and Kopke, echoes Symington when he says: ‘We had to make profound use of the knowledge of our grapes, as each variety and each plot of vineyard developed at a different pace.

Château des Jacques.zin: Cyril Chirouze, winemaker at Château des Jacques, Louis Jadot’s Moulin-à-Vent domaine, is very positive about the vintage: ‘2018 is one of the best of the past 30 years.’

Château des Jacques, situated less than 20km south of the town of Mâcon, produces two different white wines from the same nine-hectare walled parcel of Chardonnay, the Clos de Loyse: a white Beaujolais and a white Bourgogne.
Château des Jacques was originally the property of the Sornay family, who used it principally as a residence.
The domaine was purchased in 1996 by Burgundian négociant Louis Jadot.

Château du Moulin-à-Vent.zin: Edouard Parinet, owner of Château du Moulin-à-Vent, agrees: ‘2018 is a rich and powerful vintage that can be compared to the glorious 2015.’

An intriguing vertical tasting (2010-2019) from the revitalised Château du Moulin-à-Vent confirmed the latter characteristic, while reaffirming that the age-old view of the appellation as a sturdy, traditional (and sometimes rustic) wine is in need of revision.

Domaine Labruyère.zin: Nadine Gublin, winemaker at Domaine Labruyère in Moulin-à-Vent, noted the influence of a second period of substantial rainfall – between mid-May and mid-June 70% more rain fell than normal.

Domaine Guy & Yvan Dufouleur.zin: The top performers were the Bourgogne Hautes-Côtes de Nuits Les Dames Huguette from Domaine Guy & Yvan Dufouleur, and the Bourgogne Haute- Côtes de Beaune blanc from Domaine Jean Guiton, both interesting possibilities.

Domaine du Cellier aux Moines.zin: Top names include Maison Chanzy in Bouzeron, Domaine Belleville in Rully, Château de Chamirey in Mercurey, Domaine du Cellier aux Moines in Givry, and Domaine Stéphane Aladame in Montagny (along with the Montagny wines also made by Domaine du Cellier aux Moines.

Clotilde Davenne.zin: Clotilde Davenne produced a wine that would easily pass for premier cru Chablis, while the Côte Chalonnaise shone with a lovely wine from Domaine de Villaine.

Clotilde Davenne, one of the area’s most dynamic producers, is a big fan: ‘The Aligoté is filled with sunshine and always ripens at the right time to make wines of beautiful regularity and freshness.’
A force to be reckoned with in the Grand Auxerrois, Clotilde Davenne first planted vines in 1992 at what later became her own estate: Les Temps Perdus.

Domaine Dujac.zin: Today, Domaine Dujac is run by Jacques’ two sons Jeremy and Alec, along with Jeremy’s wife Diana (née Snowden) and their brother Paul.
The most interesting commentary came from Jeremy Seysses at Domaine Dujac, who felt that the 18hl/ha they achieved was respectable, given that they also maintained their certified organic status.

Domaine de la Romanée-Conti.zin: According to Bertrand de Villaine of Domaine de la Romanée-Conti, a north wind that prevailed from Palm Sunday (5 April in 2020) onward also helped concentrate the fruit.

Nonetheless, the unsurprising top-scorer was from Domaine de la Romanée-Conti, with the domaine’s La Tâche 2022 getting the seal of approval from Charles Curtis MW during his in-bottle tasting this spring.

Domaine de la Romanée-Conti first produced a red Corton in 2009 from 2.27 hectares that they lease from the heirs of the Domaine Prince Florent de Merode (in Corton Bressandes, Clos du Roi, and Renardes).
Domaine de la Romanée-Conti has released its 2022 wines in bottle and the UK wine trade and press were the first to taste them in London last week.
Bertrand de Villaine at Domaine de la Romanée-Conti was enthusiastic about 2019.
Precision was important: at Domaine de la Romanée-Conti, harvest started and ended with grand cru Grands Echezeaux.

Domaine Armand Rousseau.zin: According to Cyrielle Rousseau of Domaine Armand Rousseau, it was complicated, with 15 barrels less than average in the producer’s Gevrey-Chambertin 1er Cru Clos St Jacques [due to flooding] and two hail storms.
Cyrielle Rousseau at Domaine Armand Rousseau was extremely bullish on the 2019 vintage.

Rijckaert.zin: Winemaker Florent Rouve of Vins Rijckaert notes that excessively hot and dry conditions caused vines to shut down in August, which helped keep alcohol levels in check.

Domaine Michel Lafarge.zin: In the opinion of Frédéric Lafarge of Domaine Michel Lafarge, ‘2022 was a great vintage to lay down; 2023 was a vintage of great charm.’

Domaine Chandon de Briailles.zin: Claude de Nicolay of Corton’s Domaine Chandon de Briailles notes that the last of the Pinot to be brought in suffered a bit of shrivelling from the sun, and that the acidity ‘was not enormous’.
Claude de Nicolay from Domaine Chandon de Briailles described the season: ‘I am happy with the result: it was not an easy vintage but a great vintage.

Joseph Drouhin.zin: According to Frédéric Drouhin, CEO of Maison Joseph Drouhin, ‘2024 is a vintage of delicacy, sobriety and precision.

Domaine des Comtes Lafon.zin: If money is no object, invest in the Montrachet from Domaine des Comtes Lafon or the Chevalier-Montrachet from Domaine Jean Chartron or Domaine Michel Niellon.
Pierre Lafon of Domaine des Comtes Lafon says: ‘2024 was really hard in the vineyard but really easy in the cellar’.
Domaine des Comtes Lafon also picked fairly early, starting on 26 August.

Domaine Marcel Couturier.zin: The domaine has been around for some time, but Marcel is now transitioning the bulk of the winemaking to his son, Auxence.

Domaine Henri & Gilles Buisson.zin: Domaine Henri & Gilles Buisson is now run by Henri’s grandsons Franck and Frédérick.
The farming is certified organic, and the wines are made with great care.

Domaine de la Commaraine.zin: Although I have been following the wines for several years, I tasted for the first time at the Château de la Commaraine with technical director Paul Krug at the estate itself in autumn 2025.

Patrick Piuze.zin: Patrick Piuze picked 2014 and 2015, Vincent Dauvissat chose 2014 and 2002, and Benoît Droin nominated 2014 and 2010.

Domaine Billaud-Simon.zin: Olivier Bailly of Domaine Billaud-Simon echoes that verdict, confirming ‘2020 is a classic vintage more like 2014 and 2017 than 2018 or 2019’.

Domaine William Fèvre.zin: The wines of Domaine William Fèvre are stunning across the board.

Didier Séguier at Domaine William Fèvre summed up his thoughts: ‘I’m optimistic – 2023 was an interesting vintage with fantastic ageing potential, and one that presents the possibility of staying true to the Chablis style.’
Didier Séguier from Domaine William Fèvre, which also has vines in Les Clos, says: ‘Normally we employ 160 pickers for 9-10 days of picking.

Samuel Billaud.zin: A tasting of Samuel Billaud’s range showed why he is now considered another Chablis superstar.

Domaine Céline & Frédéric Gueguen.zin: Domaine Céline & Frédéric Gueguen’s Chablis retails at just £15.99 but shows concentration on the palate and extra layers of flavour, kept in perfect balance by crisp acidity and a fine, mineral finish.

Domaine Séguinot-Bordet.zin: The Chablis ‘Vieilles Vignes’ from Domaine Séguinot-Bordet comes in at just over £20 and offers a great deal of fruit purity and an energy on the palate which makes one want to drink another glass.

Domaine des Malandes.zin: Domaine des Malandes Premier Cru Montmains scored 93 points and will retail between £30-£35 (based on previous years prices) and considering Andy Howard MW highlighted Montmains as being one of the top-performing premiers crus in 2020, this is one to try and get your hands on.

Domaine 47°N 3°E.zin: Guillaume Michaut at Domaine 47°N 3°E agrees: ‘This is a vintage our grandfathers could have made’.

Domaine François Raveneau.zin: Isabelle Raveneau, of Domaine François Raveneau, describes the varied nature of the destruction: ‘We began to pick on 23 September and finished in a bit over five days.

It must be said that ‘Petit’ does not indicate ‘lesser’, as good producers, such as Domaine François Raveneau, William Fèvre and Samuel Billaud, all make Petit Chablis that can out-compete many a Chablis.

Domaine Comte Georges de Vogüé.zin: According to François Millet at Domaine Comte Georges de Vogüé, 2019 was ‘A subtle vintage; things were said so quietly and calmly, and there was nothing demonstrative about except the elegance.’
Jean Lupatelli, director of Domaine Comte Georges de Vogüé, describes the variations within the same village: ‘We did one third of a normal crop after sorting.

Domaine Amiot-Servelle.zin: Antoine Amiot-Servelle of Domaine Amiot-Servelle says: ‘2024 is not the easiest vintage, but I am an old-time optimist.
Antoine Amiot-Servelle of Domaine Amiot-Servelle says that they ended up with six to eight buds per vine after debudding.

Domaine Michel Niellon.zin: At Domaine Michel Niellon, winemaker Lucie Coutoux says: ‘The wines have finesse and freshness; they are subtle, discreet and harmonious.

Julien Sunier.zin: Julien Sunier, a newcomer to the Beaujolais region in 2003, says this new generation are putting their energy into organics, respecting the environment and vinifying their own wines, as opposed to selling in bulk.

Georges Duboeuf.zin: All 13 bottles supplied by Beaujolais giant Georges Duboeuf scored well across different Crus and quality tiers, while Korean-born, US-educated and French-trained newcomer Mee Godard was a hit with every wine: a young producer well worth following.

Jean-Paul Brun.zin: Jean-Paul Brun is a leading producer of white wine in the Beaujolais region, and claims that the limestone soils in the south are the reason for Chardonnay’s success.

Domaine Anne Gros.zin: I have been tasting at Domaine Anne Gros for a number of years.
The barrels at Domaine Anne Gros are normally sourced from three coopers: Damy, François Frères and Berthomieu/Ermitage (who steam the wood first before toasting it).

The elegance and finesse of the wines from Domaine Anne Gros became apparent in Curtis’ profile published on Decanter Premium online in October, and her Richebourg Grand Cru 2009 is showing beautifully.

Domaine Paul Tollot-Gros.zin: Paul has recently launched his own domaine, Domaine Paul Tollot-Gros, vinifying some of the Bourgogne Rouge, village-level Vosne-Romanée and Echézeaux, experimenting with later picking and using some whole clusters.

Domaine Fourrier.zin: At Domaine Fourrier, cellar master François Orisé says that the domaine lost 70% of its crop to mildew.

Simonnet-Febvre.zin: Vincent Wengier in Chablis, says that, ‘global warming has been very beneficial for our region’, while Maison Simonnet-Febvre general manager Paul Espitalié observes: ‘Over the past 15 years, climate change has been very important, particularly for the reds.’
Further to the southwest of Chablis, Simonnet-Febvre is now setting out to reinvigorate the vineyards of the lesser-known IGP Coteaux de l’Auxois.

Domaine Verret.zin: Domaine Verret has been cultivating vines and making wine for five generations.

Domaine Long-Depaquit.zin: It is a monopole belonging to Domaine Long-Depaquit, with 5% of it situated within Les Preuses and 95% within Vaudesir.

Maison Chanzy.zin: Maison Chanzy showed the potential for Aligoté at a recent tasting, with three different slants on the distinctive Bouzeron terroir.

Domaine Marcel Lapierre.zin: Domaine Marcel Lapierre was founded in 1909 by Michel Lapierre, whose son Camille joined him at the winery in 1925.
Camille’s son Marcel was born in 1950, and took over the domaine in 1973.
Domaine Marcel Lapierre, for example, has macerations that last anywhere from nine to 35 days according to the desired style.

Domaine Jules Desjourneys.zin: Fabien Duperray is a breath of fresh air who is among France’s foremost fine wine agents.

Domaine Laurent Gauthier.zin: The Gauthier family has been growing grapes since 1834, and today the domaine is run by Laurent Gauthier and his two sons, Jason and Elie.

Domaine Mee Godard.zin: In 2013, she acquired a few hectares in and around Morgon, which she has since grown to 7.8ha.

Guy Breton.zin: At just under 7ha, Domaine Guy Breton is modest in size but not reputation.

Domaine de Montille.zin: Brian Sieve, winemaker at Domaine de Montille, says that much of the vineyard work was done earlier to preserve freshness in the wine and combat the effects of global warming.

Brian Sieve, chef de cave at Domaine de Montille, said Pommard needed a ripe year to shine, and that ripening was aided by the dryness of the year, adding that it was one of the five driest vintages ever.

Benjamin Leroux.zin: Benjamin Leroux is a negociant with growing holdings in Meursault, which expanded this year.

Domaine des Lambrays.zin: At Domaine des Lambrays they made no changes, and winemaker Jacques Devauges describes his process: ‘We sorted like madmen, with three sorting tables, but we didn’t change the proportions of whole bunches: 40% for the premiers crus and 80% for the Clos des Lambrays.
Jacques Devauges at Domaine des Lambrays says: ‘We carried out a very careful de-budding, and normally I am not a fan of green harvesting, but in 2023 it was [also] needed.’

Domaine Ponsot.zin: At Domaine Ponsot, winemaker Alexandre Abel says that he lost half of his crop to mildew in one week, since the domaine was unable to spray due to rain.
Despite this general trend, Alexandre Abel at Domaine Ponsot was surprised at the structure of the wines.

Château de Pommard.zin: Paul Négrerie, cellarmaster at the nearby Château de Pommard, had a similar experience in 2024: ‘Yields overall were 14hl/ha.

Domaine Robert Groffier.zin: Quantities in Chambolle were as generous as elsewhere – there was enough fruit for Nicolas Groffier of Domaine Robert Groffier to offer multiple cuvées of both grand cru Bonnes-Mares and premier cru Les Amoureuses.

Domaine Jean Chartron.zin: Anne-Laure Chartron, managing the vineyards for Domaine Jean Chartron, said: ‘There was no water stress in Puligny – one could look at the vines all summer and never see wilted yellow leaves.

Pierre-Yves Colin-Morey.zin: Chassagne producer Domaine Pierre-Yves Colin-Morey was not far behind.

Domaine Baron Thénard.zin: According to Jean-Baptiste Bordeaux-Montrieux, proprietor of venerable Givry estate Domaine Baron Thénard, this was the earliest harvest on record – they started picking on the 18th of August.

Domaine Faiveley.zin: Jérôme Flous, the winemaker at Domaine Faiveley, notes the effect on yields: ‘Yields overall for the Chardonnay were closer to normal, averaging 40hl/ha, while the Pinots gave 20-30hl/ha depending on the site,’ he explains.

Domaine Trapet Père et Fils.zin: Louis Trapet at Domaine Trapet Père et Fils agrees about yield: ‘2023 is the maximum; 2024 is the minimum.’

Michel Bouzereau.zin: Michel Bouzereau describes a year that began ahead of schedule in May and June but fell behind with a period of cold and rain from mid-July.

Domaine Roulot.zin: Paul Delorme, cellarmaster at Domaine Roulot, seemed equally pleased: ‘We picked from the 20th of August through to the 29th, beginning with [regional-level] Grandes Coutures on the Puligny side and finishing on the Volnay side.

Etienne Sauzet.zin: Benoît Riffault of Domaine Etienne Sauzet in Puligny concurs: ‘The 2020s are refreshing but not brisk.
Gerard Boudot, winemaker at Etienne Sauzet, was extremely pleased with his 2019s: ‘We had beautiful pH levels between 3.18 and 3.28, and elevated levels of tartaric acid between 5.5g/l and 6.5g/l.

Domaine Paul Pillot.zin: Thierry Pillot at Domaine Paul Pillot said his domaine was seriously impacted by the frost, losing up to 70% in some areas.

Hubert Lignier.zin: Domaine Hubert Lignier was among the last to pick here, between September 16 and 24.
Laurent Lignier of Domaine Hubert Lignier in Morey-St-Denis says that the grapes in 2023 had lower acidity than in 2022, so lowering yields helped to emphasise the wines’ minerality and freshness.

Clos de Tart.zin: Clos de Tart winemaker Alessandro Noli concurs: ‘The property produced 60 barrels in 2020, 65% of a normal harvest.
Alessandro Noli at Clos de Tart describes a similar necessity: ‘We started [harvesting] very early and had a lot of fun, and we ended up with 34hl.

Domaine Arlaud.zin: Cyprien Arlaud at Domaine Arlaud says that even having carried out de-budding (early in the season), it was still necessary to drop fruit both before and after veraison, when the colour of the grapes changes.

Anne Gros.zin: Elsewhere in Vosne-Romanée, Anne Gros commented that she harvested three full weeks later in 2019 than in 2020.
‘Anne Gros is fortunate enough to have some magnificent sites in Vosne, so this is a lesser star in her galaxy.

Domaine du Comte Liger-Belair.zin: At Domaine du Comte Liger-Belair, Louis-Michel Liger-Belair was forthright about the struggles, reporting picking his Clos du Château later than he might have, and having to leave 30%-40% of the grapes from his new vineyard La Croix Rameau on the sorting table because of mildew.

Domaine Rapet.zin: Local Pernand standout Domaine Rapet produces an exemplary version.

Louis Jadot.zin: Louis Jadot makes both under the name Clos de la Croix de Pierre, rather than the vineyard name; however, since the Chardonnay stretches from the premier cru band to a portion classified as village-level, it isn’t a premier cru.

Louis Latour.zin: The main, and unexpected, exception was Louis Latour, whose Chaumes premier cru as well as the top-scoring Petits Monts showed well.

Domaine de Vernus.zin: Frédéric Jametton, the partner of Côte de Nuits superstar Guillaume Rouget at the Domaine de Vernus in Régnié, says: ‘I’d drink the 2023s before the 2022s, but it will be a great vintage’.

Domaine Lafarge-Vial.zin: This is the case at Domaine Lafarge-Vial in Fleurie, founded by Frédéric Lafarge and his wife Chantal (née Vial) of Volnay.

Domaine Mont Bessay.zin: At Domaine Mont Bessay the grapes from old vines are fermented largely as whole bunches and those from the younger vines are partially destemmed.

Château de Fargues.zin: There were dangers though – Château de Fargues sets out the issues many had to face in their vintage report: ‘Within several days, the berries reached wonderful concentration.

Château Gilette.zin: The appellation of the vintage though has to go to Sauternes – and I strongly recommend a jaw-dropping Château Gilette, that was only released on to the market in 2018 and is just a brilliant wine.

Château Climens.zin: And for once, yields were good, with Château Climens reporting 21hl/ha.

Château Lafaurie-Peyraguey.zin: My first Sauternes love was Château Lafaurie-Peyraguey 1983.
At Château Lafaurie-Peyraguey, the new ownership (since 2013) has also reduced time in barrel and adopted a lighter toast.

Cadence.zin: Established: Cadence was established in 1998 after Ben Smith left his career at Boeing.
Smith and Cadence co-owner, wife Gaye McNutt planted their estate vineyard Cara Mia on Red Mountain in 2004.
The wines from Cadence are all a product of their Red Mountain estate vineyard, purchased in 1998 and planted in 2004.
According to the team at Cadence, the physical makeup of the cobbles and clay is similar to the Pomerol and St-Emilion plateau in Bordeaux.
There may be a direction and house style that Cadence aims for, but vintage will dictate the blend.
Cadence makes a strong case for the wines that balance power and elegance with undeniable harmony that Washington is capable of producing.

Trothe.zin: Trothe founder Jeff Andrews’ family has been growing wine grapes for generations in the Horse Heaven Hills, and with all that experience, the heat of 2021 still looms as a defining factor of the vintage.
Jeff Andrews’ decision to launch the Trothe brand was based on faith in his family’s work over the decades and what the evidence was showing him.
The Trothe Cabernet is a product of some of the most select blocks in the vineyard – three in particular, each numbered for the year they were planted.
The remainder of the Trothe Cabernet blend has come from Block 03.
As the Trothe Cabernet program develops, winemaker McKee is excited to integrate some of the vineyard’s youngest sites.
In addition to the old-vine Cabernet, the Trothe Cabernet will incorporate one of the youngest Cabernet blocks on the estate, coming from site 16 (planted in 2016).
This block will become more prominent in the Trothe blend over the next 10-15 years as the vines grow up and settle into their terroir.’
Part of crafting a wine like Trothe is a hope to transport people, if even for a moment, to the sagebrush-covered canyons and windswept ridges of the wide-open Horse Heaven Hills.’
‘Trothe is part of our family’s continuing farming and wine-growing evolution,’ Andrews continues.
With Trothe, we are laying down a marker to let wine lovers know that the Horse Heaven Hills deserves a place on the world stage among the most renowned wine-growing regions.’

WT Vintners.zin: Jeff Lindsay-Thorsen, MS of WT Vintners, whose Boushey Vineyard Syrah was among the top three wines in my vintage report, makes wines in the $50 and under category as a rule.

Syncline.zin: There are small producers like Syncline located in the cooler Columbia Gorge that have made sparkling wines for a long time.

Quilceda Creek.zin: Quilceda Creek wines from this site are known for their pillowy soft dark fruit profiles with a weightless texture, as well as tar, tobacco, sagebrush and chocolate undertones.
Paul Golitzin, president and director of winemaking at Quilceda Creek, said 2020 was a vintage with ample silver linings.
It’s a classic vintage for Quilceda Creek – the wines have tremendous concentration and depth.’

Beringer.zin: It also indicates that some larger wineries, like Beringer and J Lohr, are at an advantage in a tricky vintage as they can select the best fruit from their own vineyards and from those that supply them on a contract basis.

Inglenook.zin: Yet at Francis Ford Coppola’s Inglenook, in the warmer, flatter Rutherford AVA, winemaker Chris Phelps had all his Cabernet Sauvignon fruit in the cellar by 24 September.
The standouts of the tasting for me are The Armagh Shiraz 2016, Inglenook Rubicon 2017, Galatrona Petrolo 2018 and Bibi Graetz’s toweringly good Tastamatta 2018.

Pride Mountain Vineyards.zin: Pride Mountain Vineyards winemaker Sally Johnson has a unique perch in the Mayacamas Mountains that separate Sonoma and Napa counties.

Matthiasson.zin: One notable exception was Matthiasson Vineyards, which was significantly affected by the quake.
Their 2014 Matthiasson Cabernet Sauvignon Napa Valley was among my top-scoring wines with 96-points.

Caterwaul.zin: Consider Caterwaul Cabernet Sauvignon, a $55 wine made by consultant winemaker Thomas Rivers Brown, also the mastermind behind $300+ Schrader wines.

Black Stallion.zin: Black Stallion’s Gaspare Vineyard and Materra Cunate Family’s Vine 1 are densely packed wines; both will reward upfront and also age for up to 12 years.

Lithology.zin: ‘If you look before the heatwave,’ says Lithology winemaker Matt Sands, ‘it was a great growing season – healthy canopies, excellent fruit set and well-sized berries.’

Cardinale.zin: They have a lot of the same energy, expression and life’ explains Chris Carpenter, winemaker for Lokoya, Cardinale, La Jota and Mt Brave, all part of the large Jackson Family Wines portfolio.

Pilcrow.zin: Pilcrow’s Jonah Beer says: ‘Mother Nature allowed us to walk through the vintage rather than sprint.

Chimney Rock.zin: Chimney Rock winemaker Elizabeth Vianna gave similar praise, saying ‘2018 is a beautiful, cool vintage.
The single-vineyard wines from Chimney Rock are particularly definitive.

Screaming Eagle.zin: ‘2021 required a lot of patience,’ said Nick Gislason, winemaker for Screaming Eagle, ‘The growing season was even-keeled and on the later side.

Early in my tastings, I visited Screaming Eagle and spoke with winemaker Nick Gislason, who said that ripening was slowed a bit by what he described as ‘dappled sunlight’, resulting from high-elevation smoke particles from the August LNU fires, which did not impact their vines.

Cliff Lede.zin: ‘It was a lower-yielding vintage,’ noted Christopher Tynan, Director of Winemaking for Cliff Lede Vineyards, who emphasised that the quality of the 2021 harvest in Stags Leap was exceptional.

Shafer.zin: Shafer winemaker Elias Fernandez said that with longer hang times and a perfect growing season, ‘the fruit looked phenomenal’.
Shafer produces more modern iterations, and Realm Cellars takes this profile to bonafide ‘cult’ status.

Spring Mountain Vineyard.zin: Barrett Anderson, winemaker for Spring Mountain Vineyard, said that when the heat dome arrived, ‘many vines were not at ideal brix [sugar content, ie potential alcohol] levels and didn’t really move after’.
At present, Spring Mountain Vineyard’s portfolio is quite diverse.
The Spring Mountain Vineyard estate is a standard-bearer of the Spring Mountain District AVA.

I toured the steep hillsides and craggy ranges of the Spring Mountain Vineyard estate as a passenger in Rosenbrand’s pickup truck in September, two weeks after a spate of intense heat spikes had hit Napa Valley.

That awareness, coupled with the devastation of the native forest land on the Spring Mountain Vineyard estate, could mean Napa County will permit them to plant more hectares where vines had never been planted—possibly an additional 36ha.
My five-decade tasting confirmed that the wines of Spring Mountain Vineyard are real treasures of Napa—meant for enjoyment now and, as we will see—later.

Quintessa.zin: Rebekah Wineburg of Quintessa, who produced a polished 2022, rolled her eyes at the memory of the season: ‘It was drought, heatwaves and rain,’ she said, ‘but we survived.’

Materra.zin: Chelsea Barrett, winemaker for Materra, recalled: ‘We were all physically and mentally pushed.’

La Jota.zin: Winemaker for Lokoya and La Jota, Chris Carpenter describes Howell Mountain as having a ‘gravely minerality that comes through, and a mid-palate that none of the mountain wines from the Mayacamas come close to.

Turnbull.zin: Turnbull’s Black Label and Groth’s Reserve are solid examples.

SR Tonella.zin: Inglenook (especially the Rubicon bottling) and SR Tonella are classic examples, with Scarecrow and Staglin producing a riper, more modern profile.

Corison.zin: When I started making the Corison Cabernets, there were no sub-AVAs.

Merryvale.zin: Corison, Merryvale, Spottswoode and Hourglass’ Estate bottlings are particularly classic examples of this diverse region.

Montes.zin: ‘We’d had a similar experience with our Sauvignon Blanc, so we had our concerns,’ remembers Aurelio Montes, then a consultant to Fundación Chile (the think tank that had brought ampelographer Boursiquot to Chile) and now one of Chile’s most prominent Carmenère champions.
Montes is of the former school: ‘I believe in full ripeness for Carmenère,’ he affirms.
Montes’ iconic Purple Angel is the embodiment of this style, a wine that is wildly successful in certain markets.
Montes has reduced water consumption by 65% on its Apalta estate by switching to sustainable dry-farming.

Undurraga.zin: ‘The old vines naturally produce very small bunches, which mature really well,’ explains Undurraga winemaker Rafael Urrejola, whose Extinto vineyard in Cachapoal, south of Santiago, is more than 75 years old.
Winemaker Rafael Urrejola makes wines all over Chile and has a special affinity with Cabernet Sauvignon.
Top wine Altazor comes from 35-year-old vines in Pirque and has become increasingly refined over time.
Sit and taste with him at Undurraga, in a room festooned with awards, and music is invariably playing in the background.

The TH line-up is a comparatively small part of what Urrejola does – Undurraga is among the biggest wineries in Chile – but it’s the one that has propelled him to the front rank of the country’s winemakers since it began in 2011.

Santa Carolina.zin: Other major names, including Santa Carolina, Concha y Toro and Casa Silva, are also advocates of this school.

Santa Rita.zin: ‘We have learned that you can push the limits with Carmenère,’ says Santa Rita winemaker Sebastián Labbé, who started experimenting with a radically fresher style of Carmenère in 2017.
Casa Real was one of the early ‘icon’ wines of Chile and has been one of the most admired since its first vintage in 1989.
First planted in 1850, the roots of Santa Rita’s historic 600ha wine estate run deep.
Alto Jahuel is part of Chile’s vinous patrimony and it is the main artery for Santa Rita’s 100 million-litre production – including its Carmen brand and Casa Real, one of Chile’s foremost icon wines.
Labbé is also taking over Santa Rita’s premium wines from Andrés Ilabaca, who after 20 years is now downscaling to consultant winemaker.
Santa Rita is in the middle of an unprecedented replanting programme, called WiSe (Wine & Seeds).
Few others carry such gravitas in the New World, and Santa Rita has built its reputation on this, and its other Alto Jahuel wines.

The rootstocks are being grafted with a massal selection of Cabernet Sauvignon from Santa Rita’s wealth of old vines – including the old Casa Real blocks – and other international clones are being brought in.
But while the scale of Santa Rita’s replant might be shocking, this is a company that hasn’t shied away from bold moves in the past.

Carmen.zin: From an altogether more establishment player, Carmen’s Florillón Semillon is also an impressive wine aged under a yeast veil ‘that does liposuction on the wine’, according to its maker Emily Faulconer, meaning it is ‘leaner and sharper’.

In the past, too many Chilean Cabernets, Carmenères, Chardonnays and Sauvignon Blancs have been identikit, recipe-led, often overly mature, impressive but ultimately bland concoctions that have done the country little service.

They don’t come bigger in Chile than Concha y Toro but, tasting the Marqués de Casa Concha Cabernet Sauvignon 2018 or the Terrunyo Carmenère 2018 is like discovering a new world of elegance and precision, where before the accent was on power and heft.
Its Malbec, Cabernet Sauvignon, Petit Verdot and Carmenère are particularly impressive: ageworthy, finely etched reds that are immensely classy and exciting.
Malbec and Carmenère may have become South America’s most emblematic red varieties, but in keeping with the rest of the wine world, the most-planted wine grape is actually Cabernet Sauvignon.
Founded in 1850, Carmen is one of Chile’s oldest wineries and Cabernet has always been a strength.
In recent vintages, Carmen Gold has been a star performer of Maipo, with a focus on fresher, floral expressions.
It was the first to sell a Chilean ‘Carmenère’ following its unexpected – and controversial – discovery of the grape; it also established the country’s first organic wine brand.

La Ronciere.zin: A standout project in this regard is La Ronciere’s Idahue Estate in Licantén.

Morandé.zin: Also pushing the envelope for Chilean blends is Pablo Morandé Junior, winemaker at Bodegas RE, a boutique winery set up with his famous father and siblings in Casablanca in 2008.
Meanwhile, in Maule, Viña Morandé planted Marsanne and Roussanne in Melozal in 2013.

Estampa.zin: The best examples are from Estampa, Koyle (Costa Cuarzo Sauvignon Blanc) and Casa Silva (Cool Coast Sauvignon Blanc).

Beso Negro.zin: Two wines are currently made from differing blends of Carmenère, Petit Verdot and Petite Sirah: El Libertino and El Decadente.

Clos Santa Ana.zin: Luiz Allegretti and Roberto Ibarra’s young organic project is already producing stunning wines.
The talented duo of Luca Hodgkinson and José Miguel Sotomayor (‘the Wildmakers’) are consultants, with three wines currently produced.
Old foudres made of raulí (a type of beech wood) and amphorae are used for fermentation and the wines are unfiltered.

Viu Manent.zin: Under head winemaker Patricio Celedón, Viu Manent has pushed towards lighter styles over the past five years, picking earlier and using older foudres and less new oak.

Baettig.zin: Chilean winemaker Francisco Baettig, a key figure in developing the profile of luxury Chilean Cabernet, says: ‘The challenge now is preserving acidity and freshness, the juiciness of the fruit and elegance, with moderate alcohol.
With his enviable flair for elegant Cabernet, Francisco Baettig has been reviving the overlooked region of Maule with a beautiful duo of Cabernet Sauvignons from his eponymous label.

Concha y Toro.zin: Now celebrating its 35th vintage, Don Melchor is a well-established icon of Chile.

Cono Sur.zin: Cono Sur is based in Colchagua, but Silencio, one of the top wines in the portfolio, comes from prime plots a little further north in Maipo Andes.

De Martino.zin: From vineyards in the heart of Isla de Maipo, De Martino’s Cabernet Sauvignon has evolved from the riper style of the 2000s into a stripped-back, classy and understated style.

Viña Quebrada de Macul.zin: A cult Cabernet Sauvignon producer in Chile, this boutique winery is one of the better-kept secrets of Macul.
The hillside vineyard was planted in 1970 and French winemaker Jean Pascal Lacaze makes classic, ageworthy wines, including the flagship Domus Aurea and seductive second label Stella Aurea.

San Pedro.zin: The latter was the case when the San Pedro team traveled from Chile to London for a tasting of all but one of the vintages of Altair so far released.
Until then, San Pedro had focused on more marketable brands – not least the popular Gato Negro label – with all production based at the historical winery in Molina.

Since 2002, Viña San Pedro has had a dedicated facility for the production of its fine wine range – which, in addition to Altair, includes the Cabo de Hornos, Kankana de Elqui, Sideral and Tierras Moradas labels.
The Altair brand has been fully owned by San Pedro since 2007, when Château Dassault abandoned the partnership, though with Chatonnet and Cumsille retained on the winemaking team.

Bergström.zin: He and his wife Karen Bergström both had successful medical careers and sought a family legacy that was a return to John’s farming roots.
The Bergström approach is based on biodynamic and regenerative farming in the vineyards and crafting vineyard and single-block bottlings that give their wines a real sense of place.

Cameron.zin: Cameron Winery’s renowned vineyard is known as Clos Electrique, a nearly 1ha site of mostly own-rooted Pinot Noir, which was planted in 1984 and Chardonnay, which owner John Paul planted in 1987.

Eyrie Vineyards.zin: Eyrie Vineyards is the legacy brand for the Dundee Hills, the Willamette Valley and really all of the Pacific Northwest.
In many ways, the wines of Eyrie Vineyards are historic in their own right; these bottles represent the beginning of it all.

Delmas.zin: ‘2021 was an interesting vintage,’ says Brooke Delmas Robertson, director of viticulture and winemaking for Delmas in The Rocks District AVA.
The heat dome, which Delmas Robertson references, was the defining feature of 2021.

Domaine Drouhin.zin: For the Domaine Drouhin bottling, the malolactic fermentation is blocked for the tank-fermented portion so that the wine retains a vibrant freshness.
The red wines, as in Burgundy, are destemmed and gently extracted before ageing in cask.

Domaine Serene.zin: The wines are produced in a dedicated gravity-flow winery and include a full complement of single-vineyard wines from Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, in addition to wines blended from various estate vineyards.

Evening Land.zin: Initially planted in 1984 with own-rooted vines, Evening Land has been considerably retooled by sommelier Raj Parr, winemaker Sashi Moorman and their partners.
The Chardonnay from their iconic Seven Springs Vineyard in Eola-Amity Hills AVA is a reference throughout the state.

Lingua Franca.zin: The Janzen Ranch that he purchased in 2012 is adjacent to the Seven Springs Vineyard and shares a similar terroir.
The wines are crisp, precise and as thrilling as anything in the region.

Walter Scott.zin: A former student of sommelier Erica Landon (who founded Walter Scott with her husband Ken Pahlow), he has worked with some of the greatest names in Oregon, and at Domaine de Montille in Meursault with winemaker Brian Sieve.
Walter Scott is the thriving new venture launched by wine salesman-turned-vintner Ken Pahlow and his wife Erica Landon.

The Chardonnay style here is concentrated and citrusy, with strong saline notes – the most Chablis-like wine you will find in the Willamette Valley – while the Pinot Noirs are structured, firm and dense.

Ken Pahlow of Walter Scott Wines is another profoundly influenced by Dominique Lafon, having worked with him at Evening Land and for a harvest in Burgundy – he has modelled his work in Oregon on his experiences there.
Among his early devotees was Ken Pahlow (pictured, above ), whose Walter Scott label now produces some of the valley’s top Chardonnays every vintage.

Arterberry Maresh.zin: His Arterberry Maresh Dundee Hills Pinot Noir (96-points) is only $33.50.

Evesham Wood.zin: When he started Evesham Wood, he keenly remembered his retail roots, focusing on producing wines he could afford to buy and drink regularly,’ says Nuccio.

Haden Fig.zin: ‘When I decided to start my winery, Haden Fig, in 2007,’ he continues, ‘I too was driven by the potential the Willamette Valley had to produce amazing Pinot Noir with a real sense of place.’

Bethel Heights.zin: ‘I never want to diminish the challenges of a vintage,‘ says Bethel Heights winemaker Ben Casteel, ‘as we are all affected differently; the valley is 3.5 million acres [1.4m hectares], after all.

‘At Bethel Heights, in 2021, we were able to wait on Chardonnay as late September and early October were cool, allowing for flavour development without losing acidity or rapid sugar accumulation,’ Casteel continues.

The conditions, together with the rising tide of Chardonnay in the valley, delivered the first 100-point wine from Oregon in Decanter ’s history: Bethel Heights, The High Wire Chardonnay 2023, a simply mesmerising wine from own-rooted Wente clone vines planted in 1977.

00 Wines.zin: The quest that truly motivates 00 Wines is to produce Chardonnay and Pinot Noir from the world’s greatest cool-climate sites.
The winemaker for the first vintage of 00 Wines was Léa Lafon, who returned to Burgundy after the vintage.
The grapes for 00 Wines come from the ‘H Block’ on the north side of the property that Dominique and Tarlov planted, with both Dijon clones from Burgundy and older Wente clones from U.C.

Granville.zin: Jackson Holstein, winemaker and proprietor at Granville, adds: ‘The 2022 vintage yielded some of the most compact, textured, yet precise and age-worthy Chardonnays this valley has seen.

Cimento.zin: ‘You had to have people in the rows,’ says David Wanek, proprietor of Cimento in The Rocks District, ‘and if you didn’t, you can have variability.

Argyle.zin: When Rollin Soles got the ball rolling on sparkling wine at Argyle three decades ago, who knows if he could have foreseen the growth and quality of the wine style’s production in the Willamette Valley.

Famille Fabre.zin: Château Fabre Gasparets is the most iconic wine in the Famille Fabre portfolio – but don’t go looking to drop by the cellar door.

Maxime Magnon.zin: After losing 50% of his crop in 2021, Maxime Magnon decided to buy vines in a completely different terroir, 20km away around Peyriac-de-Mer, ‘in order to diversify in terms of terroir, not to have everything so close together, ’ he says.
Originally from the Ain department in the east of France, Maxime Magnon has gained a solid reputation since launching the domaine in 2002.
But the idea is to make good wine,’ says Maxime Magnon, whose white-variety vines in Corbières are 80-120 years old.

Château Beauregard Mirouze.zin: A domaine that’s newly on my radar, this is a young husband and wife team who have taken over the family estate, converting to organics in 2010 and biodynamics in 2018.

Château Maris.zin: A good example of making biodynamic wine at some scale, this domaine has made great leaps in pushing forward on sustainable viticulture and was one of the first European vineyards to obtain BCorp certification.

Clos de l’Anhel.zin: ‘With Carignan, it’s all about yield,’ says Sophie Guiraudon of Clos de l’Anhel, where output turns around 25-30hl/ha.
The word ‘Vigneronne’ printed on the label is a declaration of her affinity with the vineyard, the vines located in the hills near Lagrasse.

Domaine de La Cendrillon.zin: Elsewhere there has been heavy investment in estates such as the Domaines Barons de Rothschild Lafite-owned Domaine d’Aussières and Domaine de La Cendrillon, but it’s the smaller domaines that may eventually add impetus to Corbières’ renown in the Languedoc.
Sixth-generation owner Robert Joyeux has invested heavily in the 48ha property since taking over in 2011.
A new winery and barrel cellar have been built and the vineyard has been certified organic since 2012.
The wines are varying blends of Syrah, Grenache and Mourvèdre, and are firm and structured.

Cave d’Embres-et-Castelmaure.zin: Long-time winemaker Bernard Pueyo has recently retired and been replaced by Antoine Robert, fresh from making wine at Cape Mentelle in Western Australia.

Château Ollieux Romanis.zin: Now a sizeable 60ha domaine, Boutenacbased Château Ollieux Romanis is a reference in the region.

Domaine Le Champ des Murailles.zin: Owner Pierre Bories is also developing another estate at Fabrézan – Domaine Le Champ des Murailles – and its Grande Cuvée was a Gold medal winner at the 2018 Decanter World Wine Awards.

Domaine des Deux Clés.zin: The vineyard is cultivated biodynamically and the wines are made with minimum intervention, but great attention to detail.

Domaine Binet-Jacquet.zin: ‘Spring and summer were fresh and rainy, ’ says Pierre Jacquet of Domaine Binet-Jacquet, and in fact there was more rain over the summer than usual.
A biodynamic domaine of 9ha set up by Pierre Jacquet and Olivier Binet, planted completely anew, with their first harvest in 2005.

Domaine de Cébène.zin: Brigitte Chevalier has forged a path within this small Languedoc appellation and has become well known for producing wines of great finesse.

Brigitte Chevalier of Domaine de Cébène admits that she wishes she had started using ceramic eggs and terracotta jars earlier than a few years ago, now saying: ‘I think that for the wines of Faugères, barrels are not justified.’

Domaine Ollier-Taillefer.zin: Run by brother and sister Luc and Françoise Ollier, this is an organic domaine of 36ha that offers excellent consistency in its range of wines.

Château Rouquette sur Mer.zin: Less than 1km as the crow flies from the blue waters of the Mediterranean, the vineyards stretch back from the château up onto the limestone chunk that is the La Clape massif.
Standing in the vineyard looking seaward, buffeted by the marine breezes, it’s not hard to imagine why the wines have a distinct saline tang.

Sarrat de Goundy.zin: Not only is the restaurant well worth a visit, but the wines are also very good, expressive and fine.

Calmel & Joseph.zin: This was the second tasting of this nature organised by négociant-producer Calmel & Joseph at the company domaine in Montirat, just outside Carcassonne.

Domaine de Montcalmès.zin: Compare this to the price of Domaine de Montcalmès at €28, Mas Cal Demoura Les Cambariolles at €26 or Domaine d’Aupilhac Les Cocalières at €19 per bottle and there are bargains to be found.

Domaine de Cambis.zin: Martin Perolari of Domaine de Cambis says it was a fight to harvest at the right time and avoid overly concentrated wines, and Luc Bettoni of Domaine les Eminades concurs: ‘Maturity had to be managed through very precise harvest dates.’

Château Coupe-Roses.zin: Sarah Frissant of Château Coupe-Roses in Minervois says they had only 250mm rainfall this growing season.

Château de Caraguilhes.zin: Etienne Besancenot, director of Château de Caraguilhes in Boutenac, is forthright: ‘We must adapt viticulture and oenology to these climatic trends,’ he says.

Domaine de Courbissac.zin: These rapid learning curves are echoed by Brunnhilde Claux of Domaine de Courbissac, also in the Minervois, who in 2022 compensated for higher alcohols in her Syrah and Grenache by adding direct-press Carignan and Mourvèdre.

Domaine Begude.zin: James Kinglake, owner of Domaine Begude, says the ‘frost at the end of April…decimated our lower, less windy vineyards ’.
At Domaine Begude it ‘prompted the vines in to ripening correctly and we picked a few days after the downpour, ’ says Kinglake.

Les Hautes Terres.zin: Geneviève and Gilles Azam of Les Hautes Terres, also in the Haute Vallée de l’Aude, say that 2021 is ‘elegant and discreet, ’ but stress that both 2021 and 2022 are both ‘very atypical vintages which really show how the climate is changing’.

Domaine de Baronarques.zin: The Domaine de Baronarques Grand Vin Rouge 2021 did have great depth of cassis fruit, but also some tight and drying tannins.

Domaine du Grès Vaillant.zin: Sadly there aren’t many producers making 100% Mauzac still whites, but those from Domaine de Mouscaillo and Domaine du Grès Vaillant are particularly charming, with some of Mauzac’s typical apple profile but also a good grating of citrus zest and balancing acidity.
A new project lead by the young Aigline de Causans and Laurent Maffeïs since 2017, Domaine du Grès Vaillant has eight hectares of vines among 70ha of woodland and meadow.

Domaine de Villeneuve.zin: Victorine Fraisse, the new generation at Domaine de Villeneuve, says that the summer saw several storms, too.
Run by Anne-Lisse Fraisse-Florac since 2005 who has now passed the reins to her 28-year-old daughter Victorine.

Domaine de Petit Roubié.zin: An organic domaine with 80ha and a huge range of wines, many of which are single-variety IGP wines.

Terres Falmet.zin: Yves Falmet, of Domaine Terres Falmet in the south of the appellation, recalls that there was ‘strong mildew pressure’.

Thierry Navarre.zin: ‘ Spring frosts meant that maturity arrived late, and there was a small yield, ’ says Thierry Navarre of his eponymous domaine in the town of Roquebrun, in the northern, schist-dominant part of the appellation.
Based in the picturesque town of Roquebrun, Thierry Navarre followed in the footsteps of his grandfather and father, who were also ‘ des hommes de la terre ’ (men of the earth), he says.

Domaine La Linquière.zin: A domaine of 25ha, it was the white that took my breath away here, Rolle and Grenache Blanc in a delicate blend of crushed rocks and apple blossom.

Clos du Gravillas.zin: New from Clos du Gravillas is I’m Alive, a carbonic maceration Vin de France blend of the ancient Piquepouls Blanc, Noir and Gris, with a touch of Cinsault.

The Bojanowskis at Clos du Gravillas in St-Jean de Minervois are well-known supporters of ancient local varieties, with Terret, Clairette and Piquepoul thriving on their limestone soils in the region’s west.

Laurent Miquel.zin: On limestone above the village of Lagrasse in Corbières, Laurent Miquel has pioneered the planting of Albariño – the popular grape of Galicia in northwest Spain that Miquel had an inkling might work in Languedoc.

Les Vignes Oubliées.zin: A sort of small cooperative where the grapes come from a collective of a few farmers working tiny parcels as naturally as possible, and the wines are made by Jean-Baptiste Granier.

Mas Conscience.zin: A domaine which was relaunched in 2020 and is now run by a number of renowned winemakers including Audrey Bonnet-Koenig, Claude Gros and Stéphane Canaguie.

Domaine du Pas de l’Escalette.zin: ‘Women removed these large stones from the vineyards so that men could work the land,’ says Delphine Zernott of Domaine du Pas de l’Escalette, ‘but they also act as barriers, protecting vines from strong winds.’

Mas d’Amile.zin: Even so, Amélie d’Hurlaborde of Mas d’Amile says that the climate keeps reminding them to look after the indigenous varieties that have better resistance to drought, like Carignan.

Domaine Danjou-Banessy.zin: ‘Old vines are like stubborn old men,’ says Benoît Danjou, co-owner of Domaine Danjou-Banessy in Espira-de-l’Agly, ‘they give what they want’ and can be difficult to manage.

Domaine du Lendemain.zin: Domaine du Lendemain in Roussillon has some pre-phylloxera vines planted in 1880 that are still producing fruit.

Domaine de la Meunerie.zin: Some white Roussillon, such as Domaine de la Meunerie’s Argenta Brilo, are made of pure Grenache Gris.

Viña Marty.zin: Viña Marty, meanwhile, is using sake yeast to enable cool ferments and longer lees ageing, for extra structure.

Viña Leyda.zin: Viña Leyda was a pioneer in Leyda, planting vines in 1998, releasing its first wine in 2001 and successfully petitioning for the creation of the Leyda Valley DO in 2002.

Casa Marín.zin: Casa Marín is the only producer here; its founder, María Luz Marín, Chile’s first female winemaker, planted her vineyard just 4km from the Pacific, against the advice of other wine professionals but with a firm belief in the potential of cool-climate wines in Chile.

Viña Ventisquero.zin: Viña Ventisquero also has plantings near lake General Carrera.

Rogue Vine.zin: Traditional field blends from Itata – such as Erazo’s Rogue Vine Grand Itata Blanco, made from Moscatel, Riesling and Semillon planted in a dry-farmed vineyard in 1922 – show a different side to Chilean wine.

Altos is focused on Malbec, especially Malbec grown on limestone soils, whereas Rogue Vine and Leonardo Erazo specialise in blended reds and whites from grapes such as Cinsault and País, Muscat and Semillon, grown on unirrigated granitic soils.

Leonardo Erazo.zin: The path that leads to Leonardo Erazo’s winery is narrow and slippery.
Wines under the Leonardo Erazo label (featuring a drawing of an owl on the label) are sourced from parcels that Erazo owns or manages himself, some no bigger than a few rows.

The Leonardo Erazo ‘premier crus’ (such as Las Curvas, La Ruptura, Hombre en Llamas and El Tunel) come from soils where rock predominates over clay; and for the Leonardo Erazo ‘grand cru’ Amigo Piedra, the soils are rockier still.

A Los Viñateros Bravos.zin: The A Los Viñateros Bravos’ Granítico and Pipeño labels (see tasting notes, p54) equate to ‘village’ wines, from soils with a higher proportion of clay.

De Martino.zin: He started working at De Martino in 1996 and has transformed the style of the winery’s reds and whites, moving them towards lower alcohol, less extraction and little or no oak.

Domaine Clape.zin: This was the first year that Pierre Clape, of Domaine Clape, had witnessed frost on the slopes of Cornas; from these parcels he lost 40% of his crop.
Olivier Clape of Domaine Clape sees 2023 as ‘like what we used to have,’ a return to wines of classical proportions compared to some of the very ripe, exaggerated wines of recent years.
There was room for a couple of top-scoring reds though, notably two 2010 Cornas from Domaine Clape and Vincent Paris, which are among Walls’s favourite vintages from that appellation to drink now.
In the north, there was almost a month’s difference in picking dates between 2021 and 2022: in 2021, Domaine Clape started harvesting its reds on 20 September; in 2022, it was 23 August.
In Cornas, Olivier Clape (of Domaine Clape) had 600mm of rain from April to July (820mm is the yearly average).

The Domaine Gonon Saint Joseph rouge 2008 is lean but fresh and appetising, and Domaine Clape Cornas 2008 lacks a little of its characteristic intensity but is nonetheless complex, with peppery herbal aromatics.
Domaine Clape’s 2006 Cornas is simply incredible and will last for much longer than their 2008.

Domaine Bernard Gripa.zin: For Fabrice Gripa of Domaine Bernard Gripa, ‘2023 was a hard vintage, but the results are not that bad… It’s a vintage where it’s possible to make very good wine, but it’s a question of what we keep and what we don’t.’

Stéphane Ogier.zin: Stéphane Ogier believes the cool nights were an important factor in the fresher style of the 2020s.
Stéphane Ogier, of his eponymous domaine, agreed that it was a year to pick late, despite the risks; rot was widespread.
The grapes appeared ready to pick very early on, according to Stéphane Ogier, but to obtain full phenolic maturity, ‘you really had to wait,’ he says.
In fact, Stéphane Ogier won’t be making his single-vineyard Côte-Rôties this year; ‘It’s a fresher vintage,’ he says, ‘and they have their place.’
The alcohols may be high in 2018, but Stéphane Ogier points out that in 2019 they’re even higher.

Stéphane Ogier, of his eponymous domaine, notes that ripening issues were more common with younger vines, and stressed the importance of fermenting with stems in 2022, which contributes structure and freshness and reduces alcohol levels.

Domaine Belle.zin: More delicate wines, such as Domaine Belle’s Hermitage and Pierre-Jean Villa’s Côte-Rôtie Fongeant, were scored at 95 or 96 points by one or two judges but not all.

Domaine Rostaing.zin: Pierre Rostaing at Domaine Rostaing describes his 2017s as ‘structured, dense, with good concentration – all we needed to make good wines for the cellar.’
According to Pierre Rostaing of Domaine Rostaing, mildew can give earthy, bitter notes to a wine, so careful sorting was required.

Domaine Niero.zin: Domaine Niero in particular made some fantastic wines in 2018, as did Domaine de Monteillet.

Domaine JP Jamet.zin: Both bunches and berries were reduced in size in 2022 – Loïc Jamet at Domaine JP Jamet says that in some bunches ‘some grapes didn’t even touch each other, they were so small’.

Domaine Marc Sorrel.zin: According to Guillaume Sorrel of Domaine Marc Sorrel, 30mm of rain was forecast, but over 100mm fell.

Domaine Gonon.zin: He prefers his 2018s, an excellent vintage for Domaine Gonon, which are more elegant in style.

Domaine Lionnet.zin: ‘It was easy to manage in the vineyard,’ says Ludovic Izerable of Domaine Lionnet, who has vineyards in the southern part of the appellation near Cornas.

Domaine Laurent Habrard.zin: I’ve been enjoying Domaine Laurent Habrard’s exceptional Crozes-Hermitage rouge ‘Kévin’ that has retained a sense of freshness despite the dry conditions.

Domaine du Mortier.zin: At the lighter end of the scale, Domaine du Mortier ‘Bara’ is fresh and approachable; Ferraton’s ‘Paradis’ is fuller in body, but its bright aromatics are irresistible now.

Xavier Gérard.zin: I’m greatly enjoying Domaine Xavier Gérard’s 2017 Côte-Rôtie at the moment, and even the 2017 Domaine Jamet Côte-Rôtie is still vividly expressive, though it will be even better in 10 years time.

Domaine Yann Chave.zin: Domaine Monier-Parréol Saint-Joseph rouge ‘Le Châtelet’ 2012 is in a lovely state of maturity now, and in Hermitage, the Domaine Yann Chave 2012 is just starting to come around, though will benefit from longer in bottle.

Domaine des Martinelles.zin: Hermitage is largely ready to be broached now, with wines such as Domaine des Martinelles old vine cuvée ‘Louis et Aimé’ now fully mature but still brimming with sap and intensity.

Domaine JL Chave.zin: Both the Jaboulet Hermitage rouge ‘La Chapelle’ and the Domaine JL Chave Hermitage rouge are at the peak of their legendary powers at the moment.
Whilst I wouldn’t have wanted to open the Domaine JL Chave much before now, the other bottles of red Hermitage would all have provided a lot of pleasure before today.

Cave de Tain.zin: And don’t forget Hermitage Vin de Paille – the Cave de Tain 1989 is still delicious, combining kaleidoscopic aromatics with perfect balance.
None of the wines were deceased, though the Cave de Tain Classique was beginning to tire and arguably would have been better a few years ago.
The Cave de Tain Classique white was the surprise of the tasting.

M Chapoutier.zin: The outlier is M Chapoutier’s De L’Orée Ermitage Blanc, which I tasted alongside Michel Chapoutier at the Decanter Fine Wine Encounter event in New York in June last year.
M Chapoutier’s white Hermitage L’Ermite is a fine showing from the tricky and varied 2024 vintage, which you can read about in our extensive en primeur coverage.

Alzipratu.zin: Pierre Acquaviva of Domaine d’Alzipratu is typical of many producers when he says: ‘I don’t find rosé particularly expressive of variety or terroir, so I’d rather make white or red wines.’

Maestracci.zin: Camille-Anaïs Raoust of Maestracci told me she only invested in temperature control over the past couple of years, as her recently retired father was reluctant to spend the money.

Clos Alivu.zin: She produces Clos Teddi, his vines furnish Clos Alivu, and I find it hard to choose between their mouthwatering Vermentinos and polished, spicy reds.

Cullen.zin: The Margaret River vineyard was founded by Dr Kevin John Cullen and Diana Madeline Cullen in 1971, with the adjacent Mangan Vineyard planted between 1995 and 1997.
Vanya is managing director and chief winemaker of Cullen Wines and has been a winemaker at the family winery since 1983.
Cullen was one of the first wineries to transition to organic and biodynamic certification.
