The closure transition has substantially improved not only the consistency of preserving Cullen’s cellared wines but also the reduction in waste caused by cork closures.
Made at Cullen Winery in 1979 from estate fruit, Cullen’s iteration of a Sauvignon Blanc-Semillon blend was the first wine of its style in Margaret River.
It was thanks to Kevin John that the annual International Cullen Chardonnay tasting was initiated, with 2004 marking its 39th year.
Vanya Cullen, chief winemaker and managing director at Cullen, recalls: ‘Mum chose the varieties to plant.
We planted Semillon and Sauvignon Blanc in 1976 in the Cullen vineyard; they’re dry-farmed and the vineyard was certified biodynamic in 2004.’
The 1979 Cullen Semillon-Sauvignon was an immediate success, taking home a trophy at the Perth Royal Wine Show.
Cullen began making a white Bordeaux blend from its Mangan vineyard in 2006, with the inclusion of Verdelho.
Cullen recalls: ‘We made separate vineyard blends once our vineyards were certified biodynamic.
In contrast, the older vines on the Cullen vineyard can handle more time in oak, about 70%, with the Sauvignon Blanc dominant in the blend.

Leeuwin Estate.zin: Under the team of viticulturist John Brocksopp and winemaker Bob Cartwright, the Leeuwin Estate name was quickly catapulted to international recognition when the 1981 vintage of Art Series Chardonnay was ranked top in a blind tasting of global Chardonnay by Decanter.
Shiraz has been the focus at Leeuwin Estate in more recent years.

Flametree.zin: In comparison to other recent vintages, Cliff Royale of Flametree Wines explains: ‘2022 sits just behind 2023 (see vintage box below).

Vasse Felix.zin: This prompted the region’s founding commercial wineries ( Vasse Felix, followed by Moss Wood, Cape Mentelle and Cullen ) to plant vineyards here, with planting material (on its rootstock) sourced from what was available via the state’s Agricultural Department.

Pierro.zin: Mike Peterkin, who founded Pierro Winery in 1979, comments: ‘It was just a logical step to combine them both when the vines were ready for their first crop.

Dormilona.zin: Wines such as Dormilona’s Orenji show that the blend lends itself to creative winemaking choices.

Xanadu.zin: Indeed, at Xanadu Wines, chief winemaker Glenn Goodall recalls that, ‘in 2022 our Chardonnay picking window, for all Margaret River vineyards, was 14 days’, compared with 26 days in 2023.

Deep Woods Estate.zin: Julian Langworthy, Deep Woods Estate’s chief winemaker, comments: ‘After the cool but wet 2021 vintage, 2022 was one of our warmer vintages.

Mylonas.zin: Producers like Papagiannakos, Akriotou and Mylonas in Attica have demonstrated its potential to make quality wines in a range of styles with character and ageing potential.
Stamatis Mylonas, an early believer whose Savatiano took home a DWWA Gold medal in 2014, is enthusiastic about the future.

Monemvasia.zin: On the island of Paros, Monemvasia (white) and Mandilaria (red) are reasserting their traditional status, where they are co-fermented to produce supple, spicy red wines with some of the silkiness of wines such as Emmanuel Reynaud’s Château Rayas and Château des Tours.

Karavitakis.zin: Another Nikos – Karavitakis – is convinced that Kotsifali, a grape traditionally used only in blends, has the potential to make outstanding varietal wines.

Caves Jean Bourdy.zin: ‘Historic’ can be an overused word, but Caves Jean Bourdy – or Domaine Bourdy, as it is now known following its generational change of ownership in 2022 – is indeed a historic domaine.

Domaine de Montbourgeau.zin: A fine example of the former is the Domaine de Montbourgeau’s Cuvée Spéciale which is aged, like vin jaune, under a flor-like veil of yeast without topping up for four years.
Many topped-up whites, such as the elegant Chardonnays made by César Deriaux at Domaine de Montbourgeau in the village of L’Etoile, display subtly oxidative notes.

Domaine Daniel Dugois.zin: The house speciality is Trousseau: nearly half the domaine is planted to this variety and four different cuvées are produced based on age of vines, work practices and different terroirs.

Domaine Jean-Louis Tissot.zin: The 17ha property is located in Montigny-lèsArsures near Arbois, an area noted for its reds – and indeed both the Poulsard and Trousseau have depth of fruit and definition.

Domaine Pignier.zin: Despite appearances (one cellar dates from the 13th century, the other from the 17th), this 14ha property has been at the cutting edge for the past 20 years.
All of the wines here are impressive; the multi-variety red Léandre the most original.

Les Granges Paquenesses.zin: Minimum intervention, gentle extraction, native yeasts and no filtration are part of her recipe.

François Rousset-Martin.zin: François Rousset-Martin who makes some of Jura’s finest expressions of Savagnin near the village of Château-Chalon, practises what he describes as ouillage à la jurassienne, topping up the maturing wine only about once a month.

Domaine des Miroirs.zin: Domaine des Miroirs, perhaps the epitome of Jura’s cult wine phenomenon, was established by Kenjiro Kagami in Grusse, in Jura’s south, in time for a small first vintage in 2011.

Caveau de Bacchus.zin: Alice Aviet of Caveau de Bacchus says that the ‘extremes of temperature and rainfall are making it harder for organic producers to grow healthy grapes without treating their vines’.

Marie-Pierre Chevassu-Fassenet.zin: Marie-Pierre Chevassu-Fassenet of the eponymous domaine in Menétrule-Vignoble describes how the ‘burning’ heat in 2022 went deep into even the marl, stressing young vines with shallow roots.

Dönnhoff.zin: Dönnhoff is renowned for its racy, elegant wines which can have a potent mineral character and plenty of tension.

Robert Haller of Würzburg’s Bürgerspital reported that Silvaner was harvested even before Müller-Thurgau, while Anne Dönnhoff of the Dönnhoff estate in the Nahe reported that fruit was so wonderfully healthy that a ‘short, compact harvest’ was possible.

Dr Loosen.zin: Dr Loosen is one of Germany's - and the world's - best producers of Riesling.

Rainer Schnaitmann.zin: Regarding the 2018 reds, Rainer Schnaitmann from Württemberg said: ‘We learned in 2003 already that heat had to be handled.

Rudolf Fürst.zin: The wines from the Centgrafenberg and Hundsrück vineyards of the Rudolf Fürst winery are also among the finest Pinot Noirs: elegant and radiantly beautiful, with tannins so silky that they seem to be wearing a dinner jacket.
Sebastian Fürst of Weingut Rudolf Fürst recalls the 18% loss in yield dealt by the late spring frost, however he also cites ‘near perfect conditions’ during the ‘crucial time’ in August.

Bernhard Huber.zin: Julian Huber from the Bernhard Huber winery in Baden is also no slouch with his Schlossberg and Wildenstein from the Bienenberg.

Peter Jakob Kühn.zin: Peter Jakob Kühn, biodynamic pioneer of the Rheingau, says it all when he notes that his usual harvest team of 25 swelled to 40 in 2017.

JJ Adeneuer.zin: Marc Adeneuer of JJ Adeneuer in the Ahr says of the 2016 Spätburgunders: ‘full ripeness, great acidity structure, ripe generosity but still mineral: I think it’s a grandiose vintage comparable to 2009.

Wittmann.zin: Philipp Wittmann of Weingut Wittmann in Rheinhessen said: ‘Indeed, a crazy year, but cool nights afforded us a vintage with German virtues: freshness, elegance and thankfully moderate alcohol levels, more classic than we all expected.

Ökonomierat Rebholz.zin: According to Hansjörg Rebholz, of Ökonomierat Rebholz in the Pfalz, ‘picking the right harvest point, not too early, not too late, was the biggest challenge of the year.’

Maximin Grünhaus.zin: The name Maximin Grünhaus has long been among the top legacies in Germany’s Mosel-Saar-Ruwer wine region.
The Maximin Grünhaus estate was given to the Benedictine monks as the monastery of Saint-Maximin of Trier in the year 966 CE.

The Bruderberg is named for the simple ‘brothers’ of the Maximin Grünhaus priory when the abbey was established more than a thousand years ago, as the wines from this parcel were designated for their consumption.
Dr Carl von Schubert of Maximin Grünhaus in the Ruwer said: ‘This year, Bruderberg was a magician.

Willi Schaefer.zin: Christoph Schaefer, along with his wife Andrea, has been at the helm of Willi Schaefer since 2015, taking over from his father Willi.
Weingut Willi Schaefer has 2ha of vines within this larger Grosse Lage cru.
The Willi Schaefer estate holdings in Wehlener Sonnenuhr are only 0.25ha.
In the face of global technological advances, the ethic at Weingut Willi Schaefer remains the same as it was in the days of Christoph’s grandfather and of those before him.
So the house style at Willi Schaefer is to do as close to nothing to the wine as they possibly can.

Clemens Busch.zin: A handful of these late releases add some depth to the tasting notes below, and in fact Clemens Busch’s Marienburg Fahrlay-Terrassen Riesling Grosses Gewächs 2016 earns my joint-top mark.

Zilliken.zin: Dorothee Zilliken of Weingut Forstmeister Geltz Zilliken in the Saar reported that, curiously, acid levels were lower than usual – still around the 7-8g/l mark, but with pH levels as low as ever at 2.9.

Wagner Stempel.zin: ‘Looking at pH was crucial in 2018,’ explained Daniel Wagner of Weingut Wagner Stempel in Rheinhessen, noting that he looked back at his records from 2003 to marvel how much he had learned since then.

Markus Molitor.zin: When Markus Molitor took over his father’s Weingut in 1984, there were just three hectares of vines, today he owns 120 hectares across the most storied Mosel and Saar sites.

Blandy’s.zin: For example, the remaining stock of Blandy’s Bual 1920 has only recently been transferred from cask to demijohn after spending a century in wood.
Blandy’s still has wines ageing in barrel and demi-john going back to the 1920 Bual.

Buying over 50% of the island’s Malmsey grapes to produce Madeira’s sweetest style, the expertise of Blandy’s shines in the precision and balance of the 1981, the last remaining barrel of which was bottled in 2019 – producing just 999 bottles.

Cossart Gordon.zin: Cossart Gordon dates back to 1745 and is the oldest company still trading on Madeira.

Williams Selyem.zin: Joseph Swann, Rochioli and Williams Selyem were pivotal early producers here, as was the sparkling wine house Iron Horse.

Far Mountain.zin: ‘The property was planted by old timers,’ says Rodrigo Soto of Far Mountain, long time estate director at Quintessa.

‘When Mai (Errazuriz) and I decided to start Far Mountain, we had the opportunity to design our wines from places that felt special to us, with positive energy, surrounded by nature in remote locations with elevation and volcanic rocky soils as the driver,’ says Rodrigo Soto.

Anakota.zin: If Verité is Pierre Seillan’s homage to Bordeaux, then Anakota is his nod to the Grand Crus of Burgundy.
Cabernet Sauvignon is expressed through two different vineyard bottlings: Helena Montana and Helena Dakota.

For Anakota, it’s a tale of two terroirs: the Montana Vineyard, at about 24 hectares, is predominately sandstone and volcanic ash, while the Dakota Vineyard, a mere 4.8 hectares, attributes the red hue of its soils to the high iron content.

Skipstone.zin: Skipstone sits on 81 hectares, 11 of those under vine, in the proposed Pocket Peak appellation in Alexander Valley.
Originally planted in 1993, grapes were sold to other wineries before entrepreneur Fahri Diner bought the estate in 2001.

Littorai.zin: At Littorai, some sites were picked before or through the heatwave, while others were deliberately held back.

Stonestreet.zin: In the Alexander Valley, an AVA where Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon are a significant part of the plantings, Stonestreet Estate Winery offered a unique perspective on how site-specificity influences harvest decisions.

Aperture Cellars.zin: This was evident in several wines from Aperture Cellars in Alexander Valley and Williams Selyem in the Russian River Valley, where savoury elements and nuanced complexity stood out over pure fruit notes.

Korbin Kameron.zin: Korbin Kameron Wine’s proprietor is Korbin Ming, whose parents bought the 8ha property in 1999.
At 716m in elevation – the highest vineyard on Moon Mountain – Korbin Kameron Wines sits about 243m above the fog line with unobstructed 360-degree views.
Robert Pepi was Korbin Kameron’s original winemaker, but now Ming, with consulting winemaker Timothy Milos, leads the winemaking with a site-first approach.

Hanzell Vineyards.zin: For more than 70 years, Hanzell Vineyards has been a revered Pinot Noir and Chardonnay house.

Moon Hollow.zin: Animals are so important to Moon Hollow Ranch that they’re featured on the labels.

Peay Vineyards.zin: In that sense, value can really be found at any price,’ explains Andy Peay, Marketing and Sales Director at Peay Vineyards in the West Sonoma Coast, before adding that ‘it all comes down to quality,’ which, ironically, is another topic that’s up for debate.

Arnot-Roberts.zin: Following Peay’s point, Duncan Arnot, one half of the duo behind Arnot-Roberts, believes that quality reflects being ‘thoughtful every step of the way.’

Ryme Cellars.zin: Ryme Cellars, for example, has been producing it for years now, successfully keeping the price impressively low for what it offers – under $30 a bottle.

Ridge Vineyards.zin: Known for its pre-industrial agricultural approach, California’s Ridge Vineyards produces estate-grown field blends starring Zinfandel.
David Gates of Ridge Vineyards notes that diversity in the vineyard fosters resilience because different varieties contribute different strengths.

Mendel.zin: ‘Pouget,’ according to Roberto de la Mota of Mendel, ‘not only imported Malbec and set up an important academic institution, but was also the person who initiated good-quality viticulture in Argentina.

‘Old vines have deeper roots and are much more balanced,’ says Mendel winemaker Roberto de la Mota, who produces Malbec, Petit Verdot and Chenin Blanc in Luján, some from vines planted more than a century ago.
Roberto de la Mota comes from a winemaking family and is one of Luján’s most experienced winemakers.
His personal winery is Mendel, founded in Mayor Drummond in 2002, with an impressive portfolio of elegant red blends and exciting old-vine whites.
He has been making Semillon for his Mendel label ever since, waving the flag for this under-appreciated variety.

Terrazas de los Andes.zin: Two experimental harvests in 1957 and 1958 were processed in Perdriel at what is now Terrazas de los Andes’ bodega (which, like Chandon, is owned by French luxury goods group LVMH).
The first of these was Hervé Birnie-Scott at Terrazas de los Andes, which harvested its first grapes in 1992 and released its initial wines four years later.

Bodegas Fabre.zin: Another Hervé – Hervé Joyaux Fabre of Bodegas Fabre and now Alta-Yarí – was the next Frenchman to make a splash in Argentina.

Cheval des Andes.zin: Philippe Rolet at Caro and Gérald Gabillet at Cheval des Andes are both brilliant winemakers.

Altar Uco.zin: Juan Pablo Michelini has spent most of his winemaking life exploring the Uco Valley and Gualtallary.
Altar Uco, launched in 2014 with Daniel Kokogian, is his passion project – these are understated yet vibrant wines, with evident mountain freshness.

Bemberg.zin: This is the crème de la crème of the varied vineyard estates of the Bemberg family, owners of Argentina’s largest wine producer Grupo Peñaflor.
Winemaker Daniel Pi has selected the best terroirs for each variety; the Cabernet from Cafayate embraces the spicy typicity of the north.

Casarena.zin: The Owen vineyard is an old-vine treasure – 20ha of parral-trained (on pergolas) Cabernet Sauvignon that’s more than 90 years old.

Viña Cobos.zin: One of Argentina’s first flying winemakers, Paul Hobbs has long been a believer in Argentinian Cabernet Sauvignon; although his successes with Malbec and Chardonnay have perhaps obscured that.
Bold reds and full-bodied Chardonnays are the trademark of California’s Paul Hobbs, whose Luján-based winery focuses on old vines in the region and new vines in the Uco Valley.

Malbec de Angeles.zin: Guillermo Barbier makes wines from the fruit of his family vineyard in Vistalba, planted in 1924.
Barbier is one of the guardian angels of Mendoza’s wine heritage, and his wines have the concentration and character that only old vines can produce.

Susana Balbo.zin: Known as the Queen of Torrontés, Susana Balbo made her name in Salta but is far more focused on Luján and the Uco Valley today.

Zuccardi.zin: ‘I’m an evangelist as much as a winemaker,’ says Sebastián Zuccardi (pictured above), staring out from the company’s new winery towards the Andes.

Riccitelli.zin: The Apple Doesn’t Fall Far From the Tree’ is the name of one of Matías Riccitelli’s brands, but it’s also a neat summary of his life.
Riccitelli Junior has been making his own wines since 2009, first alongside his day job at Fabre Montmayou and now at his own winery in Luján de Cuyo.

TintoNegro.zin: Sejanovich’s wines are at their most profound in the Uco Valley, especially from TintoNegro’s 1955 vineyard in La Consulta and the four different soil types of the La Escuela vineyard.

Le Due Terre.zin: ‘Cora Basilicata is giving a decisive turning point to Le Due Terre winery, founded by her parents Flavio and Silvana.
Le Due Terre owns 5ha of vineyards and has risen to prominence for its role in the re-evaluation of skin-macerated white wines.

Cantina Terlano.zin: I have long been a fan of Cantina Terlano’s Vorberg Pinot Bianco, so to visit this revered site was something of a pilgrimage.

Argillae.zin: I think of Giulia Di Cosimo and her dynamic management of Argillae, which is dedicated to the production of wine and oil, among woods and gullies, close to Orvieto.’
With the Signorelli 500 label, Argillae is supporting the restoration of Orvieto cathedral, which is decorated with Renaissance frescoes by Luca Signorelli.

Aroma Winery.zin: Aroma Winery, owned by Raffaele Noviello, has been able to make its way in increasingly competitive markets.’

Olianas.zin: On our island, Olianas is carrying out admirable work in this direction.’
Founded by oenologist Stefano Casadei and the Olianas family in 2002, the winery has its headquarters in Gergei, the agricultural-pastoral heart of Sardinia.

Oeno P.zin: The result was Oeno P, which he now makes back in his family’s old canava overlooking the sea.
Given the quality and artisanal nature of these wines – at 20,000 bottles a year Oeno P is a tenth of the production of Domaine Sigalas – I think these prices are justified.

Ambitious projects such as Oeno P, that aim to elevate the status of the country’s indigenous grapes and winemaking, are important steps to ensure that Greek Assyrtiko is one day mentioned in the same breath as white Burgundy or Alsatian Riesling.

Argyros.zin: Crafted by long-established family winery Argyros, using primarily Assyrtiko from 200-year-old vines rooted in volcanic soils on Santorini, this luscious yet balanced 2015 surely has many decades ahead of it.

Nk’Mip.zin: In Osoyoos, Justin Hall at Nk’Mip had to machine-pick Syrah in -2°C temperatures to get it off before snow on 3 November.

Tantalus.zin: From the Kelowna area, Tantalus Old Vines and Martin’s Lane Fritzi’s Vineyard are two of my top drops of the entire vintage.

Peak Cellars.zin: O’Rourke Peak Cellars and Culmina’s Grüner Veltliners come from opposite ends of the valley but are equally compelling.

Synchromesh.zin: The Loire-esque Synchromesh and joyfully juicy Ursa Major were immediate standouts.

Ken Forrester.zin: Ken Forrester’s The FMC – a self-confident attempt to ‘make the best wine in the world and sell it at the same price as a top Chardonnay’ – was released in 2000, two years after its eponymous owner had founded the Chenin Blanc Association of South Africa.

Alheit Vineyards.zin: Chris Alheit of Alheit Vineyards says that Chenin is less forgiving than some people imagine – the picking window can be as narrow as two days in some sites – and that the best examples need to be handled like any fine wine.

Botanica.zin: Even a famous grower such as Henk Laing, who sells to Botanica Wines, Fram and Savage from his farm on the West Coast, says, ‘I couldn’t survive from selling grapes alone’.

Boschkloof.zin: His family winery, Boschkloof, sits on the western fringe of Stellenbosch in the Polkadraai Hills, a known sweet spot for Syrah – the estate covers 24ha of which 17ha are planted to vines, about 30% being Syrah.
In Boschkloof’s cellar, the use of new oak has been drastically brought down, with open-top concrete and larger oak vessels favoured for vinifying multiple components separately.

Terroir al Límit.zin: It was at Mas Martinet that Huber first met South African winemaker Eben Sadie, with whom he first created Terroir al Límit in 2001, using fruit purchased from the Pérez family (Sadie has since moved back to Swartland to focus on his own project).
It’s worth noting that both Mas Martinet and Terroir al Límit use an element of reductive winemaking for added tension in the wines.

Clos Mogador.zin: René Barbier IV (born in 1973 in Nancy in France, home to his mother, Isabelle Meyer) is now at the wheel of Clos Mogador, the winery – one of the most celebrated in the region – founded by his father.
Clos Mogador’s Nelin has long been one of the most emblematic white wines of the region.

Torres.zin: The three towers don’t just represent Torres (‘towers’ in Spanish), they are also the coat of arms of Havana.
The third generation, Miguel Torres Carbó, ‘is the key to understanding our history’, according to Miquel.
Torres Carbó’s own ‘crisis’ was the Spanish Civil War (1936-1939), when the winery was destroyed by bombing and the ensuing years of World War II.

If you are in the US of course, then you will know Marimar Torres, sister of Mr Torres, and her daughter Cristina Torres, who are Pinot and Chardonnay producers at Marimar Estate in Sonoma’s Russian River Valley.
The change of direction between Torres Carbó and his son was a historic difference of opinion.
I am not sure he is right, because the remarkable thing about those wines is the Torres brand reassurance of consistency and consistent improvement in quality and style.

The work has been going on long enough that Torres can now release finished wines, most recently Forcada (white); with Moneu appearing at the end of the year in a red blend, and Pirene, a high-altitude red coming soon.
In Rioja, Torres is using lagares, the traditional container for treading grapes.
Torres is a co-founder of International Wineries for Climate Action (iwcawine.org), with Jackson Family Wines.
Working on a number of fronts, Torres has already cut carbon emissions per bottle since 2008 by 30% and is aiming for 55% by 2030, hence the silence of their machines.

Gramona.zin: The cousins – sons, respectively, of Xavier and Jaume Gramona (cousins themselves) – are the sixth generation to take the reins of the storied Penedès winery, whose origins go back to the 1850s.
It would be another consultant working for Gramona who, in 2018, highlighted that continuity and lineage are the essence of the company.
The cousins were therefore challenged to join Gramona and become acquainted with its operations and ethos in the hope of one day taking up the batons from their respective fathers.
The cousins were asked to step up and take over their fathers’ responsibilities, with Jaume Gramona moving to a strategic oversight position as the company’s president.
As a result of the long ageing cycles of Gramona’s wines, the two cousins are still selling the wines produced under their fathers’ leadership.

Caves São João.zin: During the négociant era, bulk wine for colonies was the principal focus, however the Costa brothers of Caves São João famously bottled the cream of the Dão crop under the Porta dos Cavaleiro brand, Reserva Seleccionada being the finest.
Well-made contemporary red, white and sparkling wines; anniversary and Frei João museum releases can be stunning.

Buçaco.zin: Retaining a foot in the négociant camp, Buçaco Reservado is made from Buçaco’s and growers’ grapes in Buçaco Palace Hotel’s cellars.

Filipa Pato & William Wouters.zin: Starting out in 2001, Pato’s daughter Filipa (of Filipa Pato & William Wouters) says she was the only new player focusing on local varieties.

Aliança.zin: As its extensive underground cellars attest, the Bairrada outpost of one of Portugal’s biggest producers, Bacalhôa Vinhos, was itself a leviathan during the heyday of bulk exports to Africa and Brazil.

Niepoort.zin: Acquired by Niepoort in 2012, the Cantanhede-based estate is cultivated biodynamically.

Quinta do Encontro.zin: Like the cuisine, whilst informed by the Atlantic, the wines (white, red and sparkling) are contemporary, with emphatic fruit and sophisticated oak.

João Tavares de Pina.zin: Playful, ‘glou-glou’ (gluggable) and natural wines have also emerged, of which João Tavares de Pina is the master, using chestnut flowers as an antioxidant and antibacterial, plus – being a committed locovore – large Portuguese chestnut barrels too.

Casa de Mouraz.zin: Launched in 2000, Lisboetas António Lopes Ribeiro and Sara Dionísio left the arts to make wine from Ribeiro’s family’s certified-organic, aged field blend vineyards in Besteiros.
The Planet Mouraz label offers pleasing no added/minimal added sulphur vins de soif.

Quinta dos Roques.zin: Structured, complex Reserva (single vineyard) and rarely made Garrafeira red blends warrant ageing for 10 years plus.

Quinta do Perdigão.zin: With its olive grove, wild flowers, honeybees and roaming horse, the bucolic, walled 7ha estate in Silgueiros, owned by architect and artist José and Vanessa Perdigão, is among the prettiest.
Organically certified wines, mostly single varietal, are full-bodied, the whites twice-pressed, the Touriga Nacional rosé oaked and reds spicy, with earthy complexity.

Global Wines.zin: Casa de Santar (classical, drier profile) and organically cultivated Paco dos Cunhas de Santar (with an excellent restaurant) are Silgueiros jewels in the crown, producing refined whites, reds, sparkling and sweet wines.

Niepoort.zin: ‘I don’t like fruitiness, I prefer the opposite – shyer, less easy, like me,’ says the former Niepoort winemaker, and indeed his elegant Dão field blend is no blockbuster.
Cement is making a comeback, used by Madeira, Raposo and Niepoort, who acquired Quinta da Lomba in 2012.

Casa da Passarella.zin: Like Porta dos Cavaleiros, my Casa da Passarella and MOB recommendations (see below) are old field blends, whole-bunch fermented and released with bottle age.
Conceived on a grand scale, this late 19th century Serra da Estrela estate was planted to 200ha (of which 40ha remain) by Amand d’Oliveira, who made his fortune in Brazil.
With winemaker Paulo Nunes, euro-millionaire Ricardo Cabral has restored its fortunes.

Herdade do Rocim.zin: First among equals is Herdade do Rocim Jupiter Code 01 2015 – a traditionally made Alentejo talha (amphora) field blend.
Aged in both talha and French oak, Herdade do Rocim Vinha Micaela 2018 conforms more closely to the classical fine wine paradigm.

Azores Wine Company.zin: Farming around 100ha has not eclipsed Azores Wine Company’s desire to single out special vineyards, including Vinha dos Utras.

Ridge Vineyards.zin: Yet, Ridge Vineyards was born in 1885 when Italian immigrant doctor Osea Perrone bought 180 acres of land on Monte Bello Ridge in the Santa Cruz Mountains.

Miguel Merino.zin: Gil is a key member of a group of young Rioja winemakers called Martes of Wine ( @martesofwine ), which also includes Miguel Merino Jr; the group meets for a dinner and a blind tasting of global wines every Tuesday, and are constantly learning from each other.
Miguel Merino Sr was terminally ill and came down to the cellar in Briones for a last farewell.
His son, Miguel Merino Navajas, is making some of the finest wines in Rioja, and the pride was glowing in his father’s features.
There are two lines at Miguel Merino – a classic one consisting of a reserva and gran reserva – and a more modern range that’s less dependent on new oak.

Artuke.zin: The basic wine, simply called Artuke, is still made as it was in 1991 (and long before that), and is one of the best-value reds in Rioja.

But there’s also a lot happening on the red front in Rioja, with ever more character in site-specific wines (Artuke’s La Condenada) and daring explorations of fruit purity, as found in Ramón Bilbao’s concrete-fermented and long-aged (100 months) Garnacha.

Arizcuren.zin: Arizcuren makes nine wines, all red: a village blend called Monte Gatún, six varietal wines (two Mazuelos, two Garnachas, a Graciano and a Maturana), three of which are vinified in amphorae, and two single-parcel wines, called Barranco del Prado and Finca El Foro.
Arizcuren thinks that Rioja is living through an important period of change.

Juan Carlos Sancha.zin: These are all serious operations, as are the likes of Bodegas Palacio, Juan Carlos Sancha, Luis Cañas, Marqués de Riscal and Dominio de Berzal among the 94 on the existing list.
‘If they start selling at €10 a bottle,’ concedes Juan Carlos Sancha, who has already released four Viñedos Singulares, ‘then we’re in trouble.’

Bodegas Valdemar.zin: A much bigger problem is that, with a handful of exceptions – Castillo de Cuzcurrita’s Tilo, Bodegas Valdemar’s Finca Alto Cantabria and Ostatu’s Gloria de Ostatu – the owners of Rioja’s best sites have not applied to join this particular club.

Viñedos de Páganos.zin: ‘A bad vineyard is still a bad vineyard,’ says Marcos Eguren at Viñedos de Páganos and Sierra Cantabria, ‘no matter how old it is.’

Remírez de Ganuza.zin: Abel Mendoza’s Viura and Remírez de Ganuza’s Olagar show why white Rioja is carving out its place alongside white Burgundy, while López de Haro’s Rosado shows that it’s possible for a wine to be elegant while also being utterly delicious.

Carlos Sánchez.zin: There was of course no shortage of gems on the red front; we were blown away by the transparency and nuance of Carlos Sánchez’s La Bendecida and Miguel Merino’s La Quinta Cruz (which also makes the strongest of cases for the potential of the Mazuelo variety).

Schloss Gobelsburg.zin: Today Schloss Gobelsburg produces over forty wines in a range of styles, but its most esteemed wine is the Riesling from Zöbinger Heiligenstein.

Mas del Périé.zin: Mas del Périé produces wines with immediacy and freshness, combined with depth of colour and lingering purity.

Clos Triguedina.zin: Initially driven by inspirational producers such as Jean-Luc Baldès of Clos Triguedina, as well as significant investment from outsiders such as Alain-Dominique Perrin (Château Lagrézette), the quality of Cahors has been on a steep upward curve for several decades.

Château Famaey.zin: At Château Famaey and Château les Croisille, a younger generation is in charge, albeit with fewer traditional winemaking links to the Cahors region.

Domaine Rotier.zin: The finest producer here is Domaine Rotier, with Alain Rotier being one of the key winemakers driving the rise in quality of one of Gaillac’s exclusive varieties – Len de l’El (aka Loin de l’Oeil).

Domaine Cauhapé.zin: Domaine Cauhapé and Clos Lapèyre are two of the leading producers.

Quinta do Ameal.zin: Having led Vinho Verde’s quality charge together with Soalheiro, Quinta do Ameal and Aphros, the winemaker is delighted about receiving recognition from big Portuguese players.
Acquired in 2019 by leading Alentejo estate, Esporão, which is maintaining the style and investing in additional planting and a new winery.

Sem Igual.zin: Sem Igual made a textural, rounded, ageworthy example until 2016, when it blended Azal with Arinto for a fresher style.
True to the label (meaning ‘without equal’), João and Leila Camizão’s label is about differentiation.

Quinta de Azevedo.zin: However, susceptible to disease and botrytis in the Atlantic-influenced Cávado sub-region, Quinta de Azevedo’s Arinto has been replaced with Loureiro, which António Braga finds ‘a much better terroir fit’.

Aphros.zin: Aphros’ sophisticated Vinhấo range includes a Palhete (the term refers to wines made by co-fermenting red and white grapes; here Vinhão has been fermented with a small percentage of Loureiro) made in amphora under the Phaunus label.
Aphros ‘Ouranus’ is one of a new breed of ‘glou glou’ (gluggable) wines.

Pequenos Rebentos.zin: Signposting artisanal trends, micro-negociant Márcio Lopes sources sappy red Pequenos Rebentos Atlântico (a Cainho-Alvarelhão-Pedral blend) from ramada vines (which Sem Igual are also exploring).
His Pequenos Rebentos Selvagem, on the other hand, is an amphora-fermented, barrel-aged Azal from traditional enforcado vines.
The name means ‘small sprouts’, but his minimal intervention, boundary-pushing range has shot to success.

Quinta de Soalheiro.zin: Home to Melgaço’s first Alvarinho vineyard (1974), the dynamic second generation makes a range of twelve expressions of the variety, from certified organic estate and grower grapes.

Fifty producers (and many more growers) account for 70% of Portugal’s Alvarinho plantings, according to Quinta de Soalheiro’s genial chief winemaker, António Luís Cerdeira (‘Luís’), who is proud of Monção e Melgaço’s special microclimate.

Adega de Monção.zin: One of Portugal’s top cooperatives, founded in the 1950s, when best-selling Alvarinho brand, Deu La Deu, was created.

Francisco Barona.zin: Among the top-scoring wines was Francisco Barona’s Finca Las Dueñas – a Reserva like no other, of robust, nuanced elegance, as charismatic as Barona himself.

Raúl Moreno.zin: I was blown away by Raúl Moreno ’s (pictured above) perfect encapsulations of technical precision and maverick questioning of stylistic assumptions.
